speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a short statement to make concerning Canada's special commonwealth African aid program.
The house will be interested to know that agreement has been reached for an aerial mapping project to be undertaken in Nigeria as a part of our assistance program. This project, which is the first Canadian capital project in Nigeria since that country attained independence, will include an aerial survey and topographical mapping of approximately 28,000 square miles. It is expected that the maps which will result from this project will greatly facilitate the economic development of Nigeria. The cost of the entire project is estimated at $1,350,000. It will be undertaken by a Canadian company over a period of two or three years, subject to the appropriation of the necessary funds by parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I simply want to say that when the minister of labour of Nigeria was here the other day we expressed our warm admiration for his country, and indication then was given of our interest in trying to assist that country in ways now covered by the announcement made by the minister.

Mr. Speaker, this is the kind of announcement that receives the wholehearted support of the Canadian people. In particular, I think any assistance by Canada to the developing nations in Africa is most welcome, is most desirable and is in our mutual interest. Our only criticism in the past has been that Canada should raise its sights and do more in this regard.

subtopic: ALLEGED SECRET USE OF EXCHANGE CONTROL FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Finance whether he will tell the house why he chose to keep the House of Commons in ignorance until June of this year concerning a change in policy affecting
the use of the exchange fund to affect the value of the Canadian dollar, which he secretly put into effect last December.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ALLEGED SECRET USE OF EXCHANGE CONTROL FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think there were any questions asked about this matter in the meantime. There was a modification of the policy, not an extensive or far reaching modification but a modification. I think if anyone had chosen to ask a question and the opposition had been on its toes, for instance, this information would have been forthcoming in reply to any questions. The position of the exchange control fund is published as at the end of each month. There is no secrecy attending that.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, I say this information now comes to light not by reason of any questions asked in the house but by another breach of confidence by the man who is the governor of the agent of the government in these matters. This is a shocking breach of confidence by a man who pretends to stand on principle and to be defending principle.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ALLEGED SECRET USE OF EXCHANGE CONTROL FUND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the minister not aware that when this matter was brought up in the house he gave the house an assurance that the exchange fund was being used to level off fluctuations in the rate of exchange but not to affect the rate itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ALLEGED SECRET USE OF EXCHANGE CONTROL FUND
speechtext: That was the policy that was observed, Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated to the house in reply to any question there has been on this subject. I would not wish the house to be misled by what has been said elsewhere into thinking that there was some far reaching or extensive departure from the policy that had been followed. It was a very modest modification of the formula that had been observed up until that time. I emphasize that fact-a very modest modification, not the impression that has been created elsewhere on the subject.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ALLEGED SECRET USE OF EXCHANGE CONTROL FUND
speechtext: Would the minister tell the house whether there is any relation between the use of the fund in this way and his description of the reduction of the dollar by a significant discount?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ALLEGED SECRET USE OF EXCHANGE CONTROL FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to answer the hon. gentleman's question clearly if I fully apprehend it. What he has asked me about is, I take it, something that occurred after December 20 and

Inquiries of the Ministry prior to June 20. I have been asked questions and I have answered questions as to what is in our minds in relation to a significant discount at any particular time depending upon Canada's total economic circumstances. That has been made very clear, Mr. Speaker. If I have not fully apprehended the hon. gentleman's question, I will be glad to enlarge further.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Public Works. My question arises out of a resolution passed by the Fort William city council urging the government to give consideration to the construction of a bridge across the Kaministikwia river as an extension of Eighth avenue to the city road to provide access to highway No. 61. Has the minister received this request from the city of Fort William, and, if so, is he in a position to say that consideration will be given to this project?
Hon. D. J. Walker (Minisier of Public
Works): Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question. I have received the resolution referred to, and I have the answer.
The letter containing the resolution of the city of Fort William concerning a bridge over the Kaministikwia river was received only today. I have not had much opportunity to study the resolution as such. However, I have in the past examined the request for a bridge over this river, which would appear to be a link in the road system of the city and province. I stress those latter words. As such, it did not appear to be a responsibility of the federal Department of Public Works.
The hon. member raised a question on this matter during discussion of the estimates

of my department on June 15, as reported at page 6392 of Hansard of that date. He suggested that a future extension of the terminal might require such a bridge. Our present plan for the lakehead is extensive, as the hon. member mentioned, and can be enlarged two or three times if necessary without affecting the proposed bridge. Our traffic connections to the seaway terminal will be quite adequate in view of the large overpass now under construction which will connect the terminal directly to the main highway arteries. The answer, therefore, is no; we do not intend to build a bridge.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF LOBSTER FISHING SEASON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on Saturday last I said I hoped to be in a position to make a report today. I am now able to say that up to July 6 the catch in lobster district 6B was about 90 per cent of the average for the last three years. At that date there were still nine days of fishing remaining and catches were heavy. It is expected that by July 15 at least an average catch will have been harvested. Income Tax Act

speechtext: Subclause (7)(b) contains a reference, I take it, to a pension plan, and the maximum that can be deducted by an employer would be the amount of the pension and the deferred profit sharing. How long has the maximum been set at $1,500?

Income Tax Act

speechtext: This is, of course, one of the measures that is calculated by the government, I suppose-perhaps not to direct; that is far too strong a word-but to suggest to Canadians who have savings plans of one kind or another that it would be desirable for them to invest those savings in Canada. That is a position that I do not quarrel with, a position that Mr. Coyne, of course, has been taking for a long time, and that the government appeared to accept from him in the baby budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS

The clause certainly commends itself to me as I would imagine it does to most other members of the house; but it did seem to me, sir, that perhaps the government was hiding its light under a bushel, and hiding the source of its light under a bushel.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in the submission of the Canadian chamber of commerce to the minister in April, 1961 they reported to him that they had examined last year's Bill C-84, and the executive council went on record as endorsing the postponement of tax on members of deferred profit sharing plans until such times as payments were actually received. Now, is that commendation provided for in this legislation to set up the new section 79 (c) for deferred profit sharing plans? Is there in this bill the equivalent of what the chamber of commerce commended when they referred to section 36 and the three year average formula?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member will look back at clause 16 of this bill I think he will find the answer to his question. There cannot be an unqualified answer to the question he posed. If the payments are derived from the fund at the time of retirement in accordance with terms of a registered deferred profit sharing plan, then they will qualify under section 36 of the act; but if they should be withdrawn before that time for any reason, then they would not qualify under section 36 of the act. I am speaking of withdrawals before retirement.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Can the minister give us just a word of explanation on subclause 8?

This clause will take account of the change that will probably be brought about in various plans following the adoption of this measure. It is quite obvious that various plans will now seek to qualify as deferred profit sharing plans under the act in order to obtain the tax advantages

provided under this legislation. This clause is designed to look at what may happen in relation to some existing plans which must undergo certain changes in order to qualify as deferred profit sharing plans for registration under the act. That is the background against which this provision is written, and this applies to the beneficiary, the employee who may have been contributing under a plan himself. What is to become now of the contributions he has made into a plan if he is to withdraw them? What is to be the position of the withdrawals?

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Upon which under the law in the past he has paid tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Yes. This clause deals with that situation and, as indicated, the beneficiary, the employee, will be allowed to receive tax free an amount equal to the aggregate of the amounts that he was required to include in computing income in previous years by virtue of an allocation made to him under the employee profit sharing plan but which he has not actually received previously. In the second place, he will also be allowed to receive tax free the return of all his own contributions which he did not previously receive and the net capital gains made by the trust and allocated to him when the plan was an employees' profit sharing plan.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: I take it, then, that there is no tax paid on capital gains in respect of any of these funds?

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS

speechtext:

Income Tax Act
How could the employee contribute to a profit sharing plan? Surely the profits are made by the employer.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS

speechtext: In other words, this relates not merely to profit sharing plans but also to a kind of mixed arrangement where there might be a combination of a pension plan and a profit sharing plan?

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS

speechtext: But once one of these is converted into a deferred profit sharing plan there could be no more employee contribution to it in order to qualify under this law.

subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT

subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: The minister has raised a point there, or perhaps I raised it and the minister has enlarged on it a little. Would the Minister of National Revenue accept for registration a mixed plan that was partly a deferred profit sharing plan and partly a savings plan? It would not appear to come within the categories that we considered on page 22 at a length to which the minister rather took exception last night. It seems to me that if you had such a mixed plan the attribution of capital gains, for example, and perhaps even the attribution of the shares of the various participants would be made very much more difficult. In other words, I think we ought to know whether these plans have to be strictly deferred profit sharing plans or if they can also have a savings element and other elements added to them without being disqualified under the legislation.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS

Income Tax Act
Surely this means very clearly that a plan that qualifies as a profit sharing plan in positive terms because it has all the ingredients that the statute prescribes for the deferred profit sharing plan does not cease thereby to be a profit sharing plan because it also includes other provisions, such as contributions by the employees; but there is no tax advantage accruing to anyone in respect of the contributions made by the employees.

speechtext: Just what is envisaged here? What type of appropriation by the employer is being forbidden here from the point of view of tax benefit? Has it reference to use of the funds for the business itself?

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Is there any control over any securities that might be held in such a fund? For instance, could the fund be made up of common stock in a company? In the case of some of these funds in the United States I believe that common stock of the company is held as security.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: We had that last night, Mr. Chairman. maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: In other words it is perfectly clear that under no circumstances will one of these plans be recognized if any part of the funds in it is used in any fashion as capital or as a loan to the company that has made the profits. maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: He can invest in shares of the company.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Could the whole amount be invested in shares of the company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. There is no limit on the shareholdings of the company.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: I wish to pursue that a little further. I understood from what the minister said that these funds could not be invested in any way in the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: The reference is to notes, bonds, debentures or similar obligations. Capital stock is not an obligation.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: I quite appreciate that, but that raises this question. Why should there be this distinct prohibition on fixed interest obligations and things of that sort? Why should it be competent to invest in something that may or may not produce a profit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: A great many of these plans are designed to encourage the employees to acquire a share of the stock ownership of the company that is the employer.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: What fear is there of having them invest in the other obligations of the company? Is this a treasury provision? What does the treasury fear may happen?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: We were on this subject last night, Mr. Chairman. It is in kind with various other provisions of the act. If such provisions were not written into the act here and elsewhere it would be possible for a taxpayer who has obtained a tax advantage under given circumstances to get his money back by the appearance of a loan. We dealt with this subject last evening. It is the same situation, and the same reason applies.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
It would appear to me to be equally easy, if the company had an authorized capital which had not all been subscribed, for the fund to subscribe to the additional stock and the company thereby to get back the money just as effectively and indeed more effectively, because there would be no obligation to pay any interest on it. That would appear to me to be as easy or easier than would be the case with a loan or bonds or debentures. To my simple mind there does not appear to be much valid reason in what the minister said about getting back the money. There may be some other reason, as indeed I am sure there must be. I am sure this was not included simply to make the bill more complicated.
What precisely is the concern? When all is said and done I assume that the company,

unless it went broke and defaulted, would have to pay back this amount and would have to pay interest in the meantime. There does not seem to be any possible loss to the treasury because of this provision. It would appear to me that it must be included in order, in some way, to protect the funds. If it is included to avoid a loss to the treasury I wish the minister would explain how a loss to the treasury could occur.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: I have endeavoured to do that, Mr. Chairman. I think the hon. member does not appreciate the difference between the acquisition of stock in a company which carries with it a share of ownership in the company and the distribution or recovery by the company of money through the issuance of what would appear to be debentures, notes or bonds thus recovering the benefit of money that has been contributed to the fund by the employer and for which he has received a tax deduction. This is fully understood by the business community.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, no doubt it is understood by the business community but I am a member of parliament, just like everyone else in this chamber.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: Not quite like anyone else in this chamber.

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext: The mere fact that it is understood by the business community does not justify the failure of the minister to give a comprehensive reason. I put this question to the minister. Let us suppose that company A which has one of these deferred profit sharing plans borrows $10,000 from the Bank of Montreal at the same rate of interest as company B, which borrows a similar sum from the trustee of the profit sharing plan. Is not the relationship of both those loans to the treasury precisely the same? What tax advantage would company B receive through borrowing from the trustee over what company A would receive as a result of borrowing from the Bank of Montreal at the same rate of interest? If that were explained to me I think I would see the point, but at the moment I fail to see that the source of funds makes any difference as far as the treasury is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
It makes a great deal of difference if you are opening the door to all kinds of transactions under which the employer is simply recovering his money and handing over what may be no more than a piece of paper, a note. This would open the door to all kinds of devices that could defeat the purposes of the legislation.

speechtext: As far as I can make out, what the minister is now saying is that this has nothing at all to do with revenue and nothing to do with the treasury. This represents an attempt to protect these funds from abuse, to protect the participants in the funds from unscrupulous employers who might borrow the money, pay no interest on it and never pay it back. Surely that would be a felony. It does not seem to me that if the employer borrows some money and pays the same rate of interest he would pay through the Bank of Montreal, there can be any possible difference between the two transactions except that you might say the employer is himself both the lender and the borrower, which is perhaps not a desirable situation to have from the point of view of the solvency of the fund. But from the point of view of the treasury, which the minister implied was the reason for this, I cannot get through my head what conceivable difference there would be in the two sets of circumstances. It seems to me we have not received an adequate explanation.

This subclause raises the question which as yet has not been answered, as to how the minister is going to find out when revocation should take place. This is a great vacuum, if I may express it in that way, in this whole scheme.
Provisions are laid down for the registration of these schemes and provision is made for revoking them if the conditions are not fulfilled, but no evidence has been given to us relating to policing and no provision appears to have been made for any form of policing of the schemes. That seems to me to be a serious lack and imperfection in the whole scheme when we are embarking on a savings plan of this kind. It is true, as the minister has said, that these are not employee savings, but this represents a scheme whereby the

Income Tax Act
government in future is going to permit profit sharing, which is now a current annual thing, to be deferred to create a property and estate which the employee may enjoy in his old age. If that is to be done under conditions laid down by this parliament, because many people are not able to protect themselves very well in these matters we should know precisely how these schemes are going to be policed and how effective that policing will be.

subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT

maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO POLICY ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
subsubtopic: INCOME TAX ACT

I recognize at once, Mr. Chairman, that what the minister says is quite true. However, I had hoped that after reflecting on this overnight the minister would come to the conclusion that the information he gave us last night was inadequate because the bill itself was inadequate, and that steps ought to be taken to improve the bill so as to provide for this supervision. We spend a good deal of the taxpayers' money with regard to insurance companies; or perhaps it is not the taxpayers' money because possibly a levy is made on the insurance companies for the purpose. However, we make a real effort to see that insurance companies in this country are well run.
The minister in his budget told us that he is now going to try to see that pension funds are better run. Here we are starting a new savings scheme on which a great many simple people will depend for their old age. Surely at the very start it would be prudent, wise and foresighted to make adequate provision for the administration and policing of the scheme. It seems to me that is something to which further consideration should be given.

speechtext:
Subclause 3 concerns tax-paid undistributed income. The act provides that corporations meeting certain conditions may elect to pay a 15 per cent tax on undistributed income which they hold on hand. The undistributed income on which this tax is paid becomes tax-paid undistributed income and may be capitalized or made available to shareholders by means of redeemable preferred shares free of personal income tax.

This present amendment, which is admittedly quite technical, provides that the tax-paid undistributed income of a corporation that is wound up may pass to another corporation and continue to be classed as tax-paid undistributed income.

This is clause 29, renumbered 28. This amendment deals with a deduction for drilling and exploration expenses incurred in searching for oil or natural gas. The first subclause of old clause 31 concerns reserves which taxpayers may deduct in computing income. The Income Tax Act, in section 85B (l)(d) provides that if a taxpayer has been required to include an amount in income on account of property sold during the year and the proceeds of the sale are not fully receivable within two years, the taxpayer may deduct as a reserve the amount that can reasonably be regarded as a portion of the profits from the sale. The two year rule is intended to leave out a great number of sales where payment is made over a period shorter than two years. It has been the practice when real estate was sold on a deferred payment basis to bring into income annually that proportion of the profit on the transaction that the payments receive in a year bore to the total sales price.
However, this concession to the taxpayer may not be completely provided for under the present law. Moreover, it has become apparent that some provision should be made to cover the method of operation followed by land development companies. These companies, frequently made up of builders, acquire land, subdivide it, instal services and

sell it to builders. The Department of National Revenue takes the position that a sale is made when a lot is transferred to a builder, but the builder may not be able to make payment for several months. It may extend over the year-end of the land company. This means that the land company has to include in income money it has not actually received, and because the term of the payment does not extend more than two years it does not qualify for a reserve under the present provisions of the act. The amendment provides that a reserve may be deducted with respect to sales of land where the proceeds of the sale are not receivable until after the end of the taxation year.

The house resumed, from Saturday July 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) for the second reading of Bill No. C-121, to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways system for the period from the 1st day of January, 1961, to the 30th day of June, 1962, and to authorize

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock on Saturday Your Honour had just drawn my attention to the scope of the bill, and there had been some discussion about a point which I was in the midst of making and which I did not have an opportunity to complete.
The point I was making was this. It is a very simple and a very obvious point, but one about which there seems to be an amazing amount of misunderstanding and confusion, and indeed a very marked change in attitude in the case of one very distinguished person. I refer to the question of who is sovereign in this country.
Lest Your Honour should think I am embarking upon a line of argument that is not germane to the bill, I will deal with that point first. The whole point of the argument I was making following the argument made, without any exception being taken to it, by my hon. friend from Laurier was that since parliament is sovereign in this country, parliament certainly has a right, before granting large sums of money to be expended by a crown corporation, to know who is going to be the head of that corporation and who its directors are going to be. That is the precise objection that we on this side of the house are taking to the government proceeding with this bill without first telling us the answer to that question.
My hon. friend from Laurier on the orders of the day this morning asked the Prime Minister whether the directors and the chairman had yet been appointed as a result of the legislation passed by this house some time ago. I remember very well that the legislation was passed by this house before the famous by-elections, because I made certain predictions about it that I am afraid are not going to be fulfilled quite literally. However, I think they are a fair indication of what is likely to happen in due course with regard to that legislation. I say, as my hon. friend from Laurier has already said, that we as a sovereign parliament are entitled to know who is going to be in charge of this crown corporation, who is going to be spending these millions and millions of dollars, before the taxpayers' money is invested in this fashion. I use the word "invested" because of course these are capital sums with which we are dealing in this bill.
In the days when the present government was not in office and when the right hon. gentleman and some of the other occupants of
Canadian National Railways the treasury benches were over here on this side of the house, this kind of argument in this set of circumstances was very frequently made both inside and outside the house. In order to illustrate the importance of the argument I am making I wish to cite as an authority the Prime Minister himself in the days when he was leader of the opposition.
I recognize that was for a very short period, and therefore I have not many citations. In fact I wish to cite only one. I have in my hand a clipping from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, a newspaper that I find very useful for reference. This is a clipping from that newspaper of March 22, 1957, headed:
Diefenbaker demands reforms-Parliament "puppet of few cabinet ministers".
In an address in Halifax the present Prime Minister appealed for:
Restoration of the prestige of parliament which today "has become the plaything and puppet of a few cabinet ministers".
I suggest that in respect of the Canadian National Railways that is precisely what has happened. Since last September nine months and eleven days have passed during which this government has declined to decide who should be the regularly appointed chairman of the board and who should be the directors of that railway, the greatest railway in North America. It does seem to me that the government, or a few cabinet ministers are treating parliament in exactly the kind of way to which the right hon. gentleman took exception at the time when he was over here on this side of the house. In other words they are seeking to make parliament the puppet of a few cabinet ministers. We are not entitled to know-we are supposed to vote this money blindly-who these people are who are to manage this railway; who is to be the head of the management of the railway; whether Mr. Gordon is finally to get out of the death cell in which he has found himself ever since last September; whether his exit from it is to be to the executioner's block, or whether he is to get a reprieve.

As a matter of fact there is many a tiger in a cage that looks pretty lively, but that does not mean he is not still in a cage. If Mr. Gordon-and I did not mean to reflect on him in any way-has perhaps exhibited some of the impatience of a caged tiger upon occasion, who can blame him, after nine months and eleven days of suspended sentence? How, indeed, can any man be expected to discharge great responsibilities when so little confidence is shown in him by those who have the responsibility for his appointment or his dismissal?

I want to make it very clear, as I think I did the other day and as my hon. triend from Laurier did, that we do not question the right of the government to replace Mr. Gordon. That is their right under the law. And we are not suggesting that parliament should usurp the functions of the government; not at all. What we are suggesting is the government should do what it is supposed to do. It should do it when it is supposed to do it, and then account for its conduct to parliament so parliament can make an intelligent judgment. If the government have found someone better than Mr. Gordon to run this railway, let them appoint him. If they cannot find anyone, let them take Mr. Gordon out of this state of suspense and reappoint him. Either course would be a respectable and a responsible course. The course that is being followed is irresponsible. It is bound to lead to bad morale; it cannot help but do so, and it should not be continued.
In this same newspaper clipping I read this:
Mr. Diefenbaker complained that the prestige of parliament had been dropping because "members were denied information on affairs of the nation".
What we have witnessed in the last few weeks and the last few months-all through this session, as a matter of fact-in the denial of information is something the equal of which cannot be found at any time since confederation. Let me go on with the Prime Minister's words:
The "shutters were drawn down whenever there was a question not in the best interest of the Liberal party."
That is what he said.

I should like to remind the hon. member who is interrupting that Hitler too won an election before he established his dictatorship, so the fact that there was a huge majority in 1958 is no excuse for saying that the government and not parliament is sovereign. This is a subversion of our whole conception of responsible government and our whole conception of parliamentary government. This is the doctrine of dictators.
The government say, "We have won the election and the other side have no rights". In that same direction the Prime Minister went further and said, "We are staying". He did not say "We will stay if the people want us"; he simply said "We are staying". His words are right there in Hansard to see. Of course we know that has happened. These people have got in office in the past by winning elections and then they have stayed and stayed without any more elections.

speechtext: Yes, for 22 years.

I say this is a very strange doctrine coming from the right hon. gentleman who in 1955 in this house, during the debate on the Defence Production Act, which was being put on the statute books solely to deal with the emergency of a possible war and only to be used in those circumstances, had this to say, and this is from Hansard of June 8 of 1955 as reported at page 4558:
However, there has been no suggestion on the part of the government that it intends to deviate one whit from the trend that apparently is to be followed, of establishing for ministers of the crown and this government an absolutism.
Those are the words of the present Prime Minister applied to the government of that day in 1955. Those words apply to the Prime Minister today who, when he is asked whether the directors of the Canadian National Railways have been appointed, on a day when the government is coming here theoretically asking us-in fact ordering us-to vote this money, says, "No, you are not entitled to this information". They said it was urgent

to get the bill through so they could appoint the directors and settle Mr. Gordon's fate, yet six weeks afterwards no appointments have been made, no decisions arrived at. Parliament has the right to know these things. As my friend the hon. member for Laurier said the other day, once we in parliament can be got rid of the government can perhaps start leafing through its list of defeated candidates and other supporters of their party to fill up these holes.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I made reference a few moments ago to trends, and it may be that I am simply following one which exists in the atmosphere around us. I shall endeavour to resist it. This opposition not only has the right but the inescapable duty to resist this tendency toward cabinet dictatorship, this tendency that was epitomized in the words of the Prime Minister when he said that the government of Canada is sovereign. Perhaps the hon. gentleman can make his speech when I have finished mine. He has been of great assistance to me on previous occasions, but on this occasion I can do without that assistance. I suggest to you, sir, that this parliament, has the right to be told, and we have a duty as the opposition to use our resources in this parliament to find out, who are the individuals who will run this railway before we dispose of vast sums of money, millions of dollars, to unknown persons. Indeed, we should not dispose of these vast sums of money to unknown persons.
There is a second point, Mr. Speaker, which seems to me to be very relevant. That is that the government has responsibility for the management of the railway. The government is not charged with management, but parliament has charged the Canadian National Railways under the statute with management. However, the government has the responsibility for the management. The Minister of Finance has denied that the government has any responsibility in another field, but in this field I do not think even the Minister of Finance would deny that he has the ultimate responsibility to this parliament for the deficit. It is not Mr. Gordon who is responsible; the responsibility lies on the Minister of Finance. The government cannot escape that responsibility. If the government is to discharge that responsibility to this parliament as it should be discharged the government must have management of the railway in which it has confidence, and it must back up that management in the way it should be backed up, or it should get rid of it.
I remember very often Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, who had a very different conception of the relationship between the government and parliament and a very different conception of the responsibility of government for agencies under its control, saying in this house that we must either have confidence in the management of the railway or we

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with considerable interest to the speech just made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, and I listened with equal interest to the several statements made on Saturday by some hon. members, notably the hon. member for Laurier. The issue before

us at this moment is a simple one. We are being asked to provide very considerable sums of money under this bill which is to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways system for the period from the 1st day of January, 1961, to the 30th day of June, 1962, and to authorize the guarantee by Her Majesty of certain securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railway Company.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has just contended that before voting these moneys we should learn from the administration what its intentions are with regard to the president, whoever he shall be, of the Canadian National Railways. We are also asking who are to be appointed to fill certain vacancies on the board of directors of this great national railway system. This is not an unusal request under any circumstances, but in the circumstances that now attend the situation with regard to the direction of this railroad I think our justification for asking for this information is great.
We are reminded that the term of office of the president of Canadian National Railways, Mr. Donald Gordon, expired some nine months ago, and that he has been carrying on, I think one may say, on sufferance during this period without any indication whether or not his term of office is to be extended of whether in fact he is to be reappointed for a fixed term under the statute. The Canadian National Railways is a large operation, the largest railway system in the world, yet for some reason this government refuses to indicate whether it proposes to continue the present president in the direction of this railroad. That is an impossible situation.
There are limits on the prerogatives, even by custom, to which a government can legitimately cling. No government can be forced to announce the appointment of a particular individual unless it has been given ample opportunity to make up its mind. But that cannot be contended in this case, because the definite term of the president expired nine months ago. Is it fair to this railway system, is it fair to this parliament, is it fair to this country that this uncertainty should prevail?
The hon. member for Bovavista-Twillingate says you have asked for certain moneys, and before those moneys are granted we are entitled to know who is going to direct the operations connected with the moneys to be appropriated under this bill. This is a reasonable request. I well remember, during the course of another debate this session, attacks were made on the president of the Canadian National Railways largely by members who sit

behind the treasury benches. The Minister of Transport was Anally prevailed upon to come to the defence of an official who serves under him.
It took some pressure to convince the Minister of Transport that it was not fair for a minister to refrain from commenting on attacks that had been made on an official who reports to parliament through him. Finally, after a long and protracted debate, the Minister of Transport manfully acknowledged that as far as he was concerned he had nothing but high commendation for the president of Canadian National Railways. But he qualified his tribute by saying "as far as I am concerned". The hon. gentleman did to an extent meet the tradition that it is always incumbent upon a minister to defend a public official with whom he has official connections, but the minister would not go further than to say "as far as I am concerned".
What we are entitled to know now is what is the regard that this government has for the president of Canadian National Railways? It can express its view as to his competence by giving us some definite indication of what it intends to do by way of reappointment or by way of replacement, but surely we are entitled to have this information. Why has the government not made up its mind, if that is the situation? If it has made up its mind, why should it not tell this house? If it has not made up its mind, then it surely owes to parliament some explanation for this long delay in determining if Mr. Donald Gordon is the kind of man it wishes to see continued as the president of Canadian National Railways.
There is a further principle involved. It is connected with other situations that have nothing to do, of course, with the operation of the railroad. It is that more and more in this country there is a growing feeling, justified or not, that the government is not satisfied with the heads of certain crown corporations, with certain leading public servants.

Surely he cannot now take the position that he can go on denying to us knowledge of the government's intention, particularly when we are now approaching the end of the present session or the present portion of this session of parliament. Is the government going to take the position that it will make an announcement with regard to the president of the railroad and the nomination of the new directors after parliament will have risen and before parliament returns? Is the government going to take advantage of that interval to announce if Mr. Gordon is going to be retained and who the new directors are? If that is the decision the government proposes to take I will say now that it will be a demonstration of this government's disregard for parliament. We cannot tell the house who the new president is going to be or whether Mr. Gordon is going to be continued or who the new directors are to be." Let the minister take the house into his confidence. But to deny us this information at this time is incomprehensible.
Let the people of this country recognize and recall the fact that we are not asking for something to be settled that has only suddenly arisen but rather something that has been in existence now for almost nine months. The hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Kootenay West spoke briefly agreeing, in effect, to the proposition as put forward in order that business proceed. Thereafter, sir, we had lengthy speeches by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), which speech appears at page 7322 of Hansard; then the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne), at page 7326; then the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Biggs) at page 7327; then the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent), at page 7330; and then the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Gundlock), at page 7333 and he concluded only because it was five o'clock. I submit that a study of those pages of Hansard indicates that this administration was not prepared to proceed with real business that day. We sat and listened to congratulatory speeches which contained nothing serious at all. I refer to the time-wasting speeches that were made in this house on that bill after the hon. member for Kootenay West concluded his remarks.
Now, sir, this is not a theoretical railroad to the Northwest Territories; it is the C.N.R., the most important link in our nation. It is one of the most important instruments of our economy and of our way of life. Surely we have the right to question the administration on some of these matters, having in mind the context of other developments in the last few weeks. These things cannot be forgotten when we ask questions now. We do not know who is going to preside over this great business in our country today. I point out, sir, this is not a case of railway business simply seen in isolation. The economic value of the C.N.R. to our community is determined not by the railway's income account and balance sheet but by the social dividends the community receives in reduced costs of transportation. The primary dividend is the money saved by using rail transport rather than any other kind of transport. I am reading these words from the study of the Canadian National Railways, volume I, by G. R. Stevens.
You will recall, sir, that Mr. Gordon received his appointment on January 1, 1950. When he took over from his eminent and 90205-6-497J
Canadian National Railways worthy predecessor, Robert Charles Vaughan, there was a deficit from the preceding year of $42 million. By great energy and devotion the new president was able to reduce that deficit immediately to something slightly over $3 million. It increased to $15 million, and thereafter for two years he was able to operate this great line at a surplus to this country. There was a slight deficit in 1954 and then for two years, until this government took over, we were operating in the black. Commencing in 1957 we find the situation where the railroad under this administration starts to slip. But what didn't slip? From a deficit of approximately $29 million they now creep up to the end of 1960 with a deficit of $67,497,000. Nevertheless under Mr. Gordon's administration we have been able to increase our operating revenues by 38 per cent and at the same time increase the average hourly earnings per employee by over 77 per cent.
We know nothing about what is going to happen in the future. We are seriously and earnestly concerned about what is going to happen to perhaps the greatest industry of our country, an industry not only important for its own sake but because it is the framework, the sinew, the arterial system for everything else in Canada. Probably there are no two things as important to the general prosperity as transportation and currency. These are the reasons why we rise today, not for the purpose of delaying the house but to put before parliament legitimately some of those problems that are very much in the minds of members of the opposition if not in the minds of members of the administration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I embark on the subject that is before us today I should like to make a few remarks in my native tongue.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in any discussion during this session which, I think, could be adjourned any moment now, but instead I wanted to listen, observe and take my bearings. So, I am not following the tradition of this house according to which the maiden speech of a new member should deal mainly with his constituency. I defer that to some later occasion. In the meantime, I will endeavour to set the record straight about the Restigouche-Madawaska election. In fact, Hansard contains some erroneous remarks made by certain opposition members.
Mr. Speaker, I do not need to acquaint the house today with the Restigouche-Madawaska

Canadian National Railways constituency. For years, that constituency was neglected and forgotten by Liberal representatives, but my predecessor, Mr. Van Horne, took it out of the Liberal party muck to restore it to its lawful place. I am determined to see to it that it retains that place.
(Text):
I have sat in the house for 17 days, Mr. Speaker, and, as I said in French a minute ago, I have been making observations and listening to the debates. Sometimes I have found them very interesting and instructive, especially when the speakers have been on the government side, but I am afraid that I cannot pay the same compliment to the opposition as on many occasions their arguments are shocking, degrading and do not add to the dignity of the house, especially when the frontbenchers are trying to overrule the Speaker.
In listening to this debate on the C.N.R. I am sure my knowledge is very limited as I was not privileged to attend the committee meetings. However, I should like to make a few observations. My riding of Restigouche-Madawaska used to have two major C.N.R. railway centres, Edmundston and Campbell-ton. They were two divisional points with a great number of people employed there but today they are largely ghost shops.
In the early fifties under Liberal management an overnight transformation to diesel power took place which should have been carried out at a much slower rate in order to save millions of horsepower. I am referring to steam engines, most of which were practically new but had to go to the scrap pile at the expense of the taxpayers. If the transformation had been carried out more slowly management would have had ample time to transfer some of the men to other departments instead of throwing them out on the street without jobs. The machinery to bring about this sudden transformation was established under the Liberal administration.
Today the government is rebuilding those two centres. I wish to compliment the government on the new station which has been built at Edmundston, a station which was in the Liberal platform for some 30 years. It was built by this government in 1959 and included a freight shed which had also been promised by the Liberals. In Campbellton a complete new transformation is to be started in the near future.
There is one major problem, Mr. Speaker, which seems to puzzle me and to puzzle all the taxpayers of Canada. It is the difference between authority and management. Last Friday in the house some hon. members made reference to some dispute involving

the private trucking companies and competition in the trucking business by the C.N.R. The answer given by the Minister of Transport was, "This is a decision for the authorities".
I have no doubt that this good and conscientious minister has inherited such a situation as a result of 22 long years of Liberal administration when authorities, management, administrations and politicians were all riding in the same private car. My question to you, sir, is this. Are we asked to vote several hundred millions of dollars to be spent by this so-called authority while at the same time we, the government members, not the opposition, have no authority as to where and how such expenditures will be made?
I am sure everyone in this house will agree that somewhere along the line there is confusion, and under our democratic system I am sure that those elected by the majority vote of the taxpayers, who have been given the responsibility by the taxpayers to vote these moneys, should have some authority with regard to how and where they will be spent. If not, then some better understanding should be in order.
There are many instances I could mention at this time where the so-called responsible authorities in the C.N.R. have cost the taxpayers of Canada thousands of dollars, if not millions. There is concrete evidence that authorities, administration and management are not working hand in hand to save public money. I know these are matters for committee meetings, Mr. Speaker, and I will not discuss them further now.
There is more than money involved in administration. Such things are involved as co-ordination of various departments, duplication of services, spending within the revenue, and public relations, and on the last topic I wish to make a few comments.
Every time the working force of the C.N.R. has received an increase in salary or an adjustment of some sort through the efforts of their unions the price has always been a mass lay-off that followed. This, Mr. Speaker, is again a sign of poor administration. If those men were needed before the increase in salaries why were they not needed after the increase was granted, or were they fired for political motives or motives of revenge? If the management of the C.N.R. would put half the effort they are now expending on firing employees on the promotion of jobs we would have better public relations than exist now between the employees and the management.
But what can we do? Under the long regime of Liberal administration the C.N.R. got out of control and it will take some time

to bring it back to where it should be. Let this so-called authority not forget that under our democratic system our elected members of the government are the ones who are responsible to the people, that the elected members of the government are responsible to the people of Canada and that the so-called authority is only authority under the duly elected members of the government.
The C.N.R. is Canada's largest business. It is spread from coast to coast and involves all classes of society and all walks of life. Again, I agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Port Arthur, as found on page 7740 of Hansard, when he quoted Mr. G. R. Stevens as having said:
The economic value of a railway to the community is determined not by the railway's income account and balance sheet, but by the social dividends the community receives from the reduced cost of transportation.
I would add that it is also determined by the services rendered to the community and I think this is the most important criterion. We have no objection to voting the necessary funds to keep this railroad operating for the welfare of the community and to offer a balanced service throughout the country, but we do take strong objection to voting money which will be spent by irresponsible so-called authorities. I refer again to the matter of trucking which I mentioned a while ago. I would suggest that for some time yet the C.N.R. should not go too strongly into the trucking business but rather should approach the matter with moderation. Since last year's operations were not too successful, and before we find ourselves with another hungry child which will have to be fed with taxpayers' money, I would suggest that effort should be made by the railways to keep their box cars filled and moving on the railroad, rather than moving them onto our highways.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that my three weeks in this house have revealed some things to me which I never expected to see and of which I am sure the people of Canada are not aware. I refer to the behaviour of the opposition in this house and to some statements made in this house about this bill. Who do they think they are, Mr. Speaker? Do they think they are still the government? Do they not remember the shocking [DOT] events of 1957 and the disaster of 1958 when the people of Canada told them on what side of the house to sit for some time to come? This time may prove to be much longer than they expect if they continue to filibuster the proceedings of this house. If the people of Canada could only see them. No one will deny that Liberal politics have been placed ahead of the interests of the country at the taxpayers' expense.
Canadian National Railways
Is this government responsible to the opposition or is it responsible to the people of Canada? Is the Canadian National responsible to the government or to the opposition? Who makes the appointments to the Canadian National Railways, the government or the opposition? Who runs the affairs of the country, the government or the opposition? Let us vote on this bill and let us keep a close watch on the expenses. In closing, let me remind my hon. friends of the opposition that instead of giving advice to this house they should direct their efforts to organizing their own camp.

speechtext:
It is too bad the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) was not here when the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) made their speeches. He could then have realized that it is the Conservative members who are filibustering on this bill.
For some time, the government has been threatening everybody. Nobody is allowed to make any speech, to criticize the government, to oppose its views.
For some time, Mr. Speaker, the government has been asking that everything goes according to its views, to its fancies. It will not allow the opposition to criticize the policy of the government, which for four years has been made up of confusion, obstruction, vision and contradiction.
I do not know what is happening now but even this bill is not supported by each and every Conservative member. Some are in favour, some are against. In a word, nobody knows where we are going. Does the government support its backbenchers who are criticizing Mr. Gordon? Does the government support Mr. Gordon? Does it reject him? We do not know.
And we are asked to vote the considerable amount of $178 million without being told whether Mr. Gordon will remain in his position or whether he will be fired.
If we are to believe the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), Mr. Gordon is public enemy No. 1 in this country. He is asking nothing less than his resignation, as we can see at page 6039 of Hansard, where the hon. member charges Mr. Gordon with being autocratic.
He is enemy No. 1 of national unity.
He asks the government not to renew Mr. Gordon's mandate.
If those assertions are accurate, what is the government waiting for? If they were accurate last year, why did it not act last year? If they were accurate two years ago, why did it not act two years ago.
The president of the Canadian National Railways is managing millions, hundreds of millions of dollars of the taxpayers, should I say, since the railway shows a deficit every year and that president is hired only from day to day.
His term of office is over. We do not know whether he is going to be president of the C.N.R. tomorrow or the day after tomorrow. And in spite of that, we are asked to vote a sum of $178 million without knowing who is going to see to it that the amount is well spent.

Mr. Speaker, suppose you are a shareholder of a company. You would certainly like to know who would manage the thousands of dollars you would invest in it.

speechtext: It certainly would not be the Liberals.

speechtext:
It seems but reasonable and fair that the country be told now, before a sum of $178 million is committed to the care of an unknown individual. The house is entitled to know who will be president and also the names of the five new directors the government intends to appoint. We do not know where we are going. We are on tender-hooks. Yesterday, a president was fired. Today another one is on the point of being fired. There are threats of a reform or of the abolition of the Senate. They threaten us with an election. But, Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that we do not fear an election. I would like action to be taken on these threats about a general election, because if there were a general election this year, I am sure the people would be glad to rid themselves as soon as possible of a government which has so badly administered the country during four years. The Liberal party, which would then replace it, would tell the house who would be appointed president, who would be appointed directors, and if a president or director were not suitable, it would dismiss him if he deserved it but it would give him a chance to defend himself before the house.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with those of my colleagues who have spoken on this amendment and to deal with a number of matters that have come up and which, in my opinion, are nothing more nor less than pretexts on the part of the government. It is unfortunate that the Minister of Finance, after having warned the house of the importance of this bill, should have left the house abruptly. It would have been much more satisfying to me were he in his seat now because there are certain things I should like to say to him in answer to the charges which he made and which I think need to be said on this occasion.
The Minister of Finance said that it was essential that this measure be carried without

delay. Why is it so essential at this time? It was in the power of the government to bring this measure before the house many weeks ago, in fact several months ago; but suddenly the Minister of Finance sees great urgency in the measure. He goes further; he warns and even threatens the opposition that, unless this legislation is passed, the operations of the Canadian National Railways will be hampered. He says this is no time for willful obstruction on the part of the opposition. May I say that the operations of the C.N.R. will go on notwithstanding the warnings and threats of the Minister of Finance. Whether this bill is delayed another day or two is a matter that will not affect the operations of the Canadian National Railways, and no one knows that better than does the Minister of Finance. After all, this great railway has been hampered by the present administration in the fact that the committee dealing with the annual report of the C.N.R. and T.C.A. met this year many weeks, in fact months, after the time at which it normally meets.
Then the Minister of Finance made this rather strange assertion. "Why", said he, "have the directors of the Canadian National Railways not been named? They cannot be named unless this legislation is proclaimed." That is not so. That is an untrue statement and no one knows it better than does the Minister of Finance.

speechtext: Order. I question whether the hon. member meant that sequence to his remarks. He said first it is an untrue statement. Then he said the minister knew it was an untrue statement. I would hope he would not leave that on the record because that is contrary to all the rules.

If you feel that, in the remarks I have made, such is the case, I of course amend them immediately. What I had in mind, however, and what I intended to say was that the statement made by the Minister of Finance was wholly inaccurate. It is not a fact to say in this house that the directors of the Canadian National Railways cannot be named until this legislation is proclaimed. That is not a fact. That is not so. That is the same old story that we were given when we asked the Minister of Transport why the directors of the Canadian National Railways were not named for days after the legislation increasing the directors from seven to 12 was passed. We were told then, "Wait until the committee has
Canadian National Railways dealt with the annual report of the C.N.R.". Now that the last piece of legislation dealing with the affairs of the Canadian National Railways is before the house we are told "Oh, no; you cannot have this information until the legislation is proclaimed". That is not so. It is not a fact. It is an inaccurate statement by the Minister of Finance and I say to the Minister of Finance that no one knows better than he does that the statement is inaccurate.

Just a moment. The minister asked me a question and I am going to reply to him. The opposition is not in possession of the information. The government is in possession of the information. The government knows whether or not the legislation has been proclaimed. However, that is not what the Minister of Finance said. I took down his words. He said that the directors of the Canadian National Railways cannot be named or appointed until this legislation is proclaimed; not until the other legislation is proclaimed but until this legislation is proclaimed. I say that statement is not accurate.
Then I return to the statement I made earlier, namely that all of this fuss could have been avoided a long time ago if the government had only had its legislation in order. However, such was not the case. The government has been bungling all along. It has not been prepared. Its legislation was not prepared for the house. Even the bill which the Minister of Transport brought down the other day was not ready. The resolution was ready and then it was based on an agreement which had not yet been made between the parties.

speechtext: There is nothing wrong with that.

speechtext:
There is a great deal wrong with that and I will tell the minister why there is a great deal wrong with it. The bargaining position of the government of Canada is being endangered by bringing into the House of Commons a resolution based upon

Canadian National Railways an agreement which has not yet been negotiated. In other words, now the parties to the construction of this railway know on the one hand that the government is going ahead with it and this knowledge will strengthen their hand in bargaining powers as between themselves on the one side and the government on the other. That is why I say it is bad business on the part of any government or any administration to bring in a resolution that is based on an agreement that has not been completed.
The hon. member for Greenwood rose in his place in this debate as he had a perfect right to do, and he said he found it strange that in regard to this routine matter there should be such a long discussion about this bill which involves the expenditure of some $180 million. He also suggested that the president and the director not being known had nothing to do with the legislation before the house. He referred to his experience in the past and I may say that he has a great deal of experience. I say to him in fairness that no one has criticized the refinancing legislation of the Canadian National Railways more constructively than has the hon. member for Greenwood. But when he makes the statement he made a while ago I say this to him. The circumstances today and the circumstances yesterday are entirely different. In past years under a Liberal administration there was no question as to who was to be the director and the president of the Canadian National Railways. At the present time there is a question. Before we vote these huge sums of money I say that we are entitled to know why it is that the government will not make up its mind and will not tell parliament.
There is a great deal in what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said earlier today, namely that the reason is, as the Prime Minister said when he was leader of the opposition, that parliament is a puppet. That is the reason. In the view of hon. gentlemen opposite parliament is exactly what the Prime Minister said; there are two sovereignties. As far as I am concerned, there is only one sovereignty and that is parliament and parliament alone. Before we vote these huge sums of money we should be entitled to know who the people are who are going to spend these sums of money.

I think the hon. member wishes to be fair. However, he has entirely ignored what was perhaps my strongest point,

namely that a committee of this house has been over these figures and has approved them.
While I am on my feet may I ask another question? Does the hon. member, with his experience, not agree that the passing of this bill is necessary in order that the arrangements for financing and so on, with which he is so familiar, can go forward? They cannot go forward, as I understand it, until this bill is passed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, that is quite correct; but what difference does it make whether it goes forward today or next week? Why is it that legislation was brought down in this house six months ago, was dealt with in stages and was not completed until last week? Whose fault is that? That is of course the fault of the government. It is also the fault of the government that we have this situation in connection with the C.N.R. If the committee had met earlier, if the affairs concerning the Canadian National Railways had been dealt with earlier we would have disposed of this matter a long time ago.
Mr. Speaker, I was passing on to another matter with which I wished to deal before I closed my remarks. It has to do with the report of the royal commission on transportation. That report, as the house knows, has been submitted to the government in at least its first part and two other volumes will be brought before the house in due course.
In this first volume it has been recommended that large sums of money be paid to the railways in four fields. First in the field of passenger train service, where the Canadian National Railways testified that their train service deficit in 1958 was $40 million, and where the Canadian Pacific Railways testified to the same effect, that their passenger train service burden in 1958 was in the neighbourhood of $15 million to $16 million, and wherein too the MacPherson commission recommended large, maximum annual payments in respect of this loss of service ranging from $40 million in 1961 to $8 million in 1965.
The second recommendation in the report had to do with light density lines and therein, too, was a recommendation for a subsidy. That also applies to export grain traffic, where the commission has recommended that in the case of C.P.R. a sum of $9 million annually shall be paid on behalf of the export grain traffic as a contribution to constant costs. There is one other matter having to do with statutory free transportation.
I raise this matter because there is to be found in the supplementary estimates of the Department of Transport an amount of $50 million which has not yet been reached during the discussion of these estimates. I

have tried to obtain information as to what this sum represents. Does it represent a partial acknowledgement or acceptance of the recommendations of the royal commission? Does it represent a payment for the wages in connection with the dispute between Canadian National Railways and its non-operating employees, or does it represent a straight subsidy in connection with both?
I think the house is entitled to receive that information before we vote on this amendment, and on the bill, if need be. I attempted to obtain this information from the committee when it dealt with the annual report of the Canadian National Railways, but again I did not get very far in that attempt because it was felt that questions relating to this matter were very close to the borderline because the commission had not yet finally reported, and in any event the wording of this item in the estimates, No. 590, was such that it was clear.
Well, I never thought it was clear at any juncture. If there ever was evidence of lack of clarity, it is in this item. I should now like to read it into Hansard. It is entitled, "Board of transport commissioners". The item reads:
Interim payments, related to recommendations of the royal commission on railway problems pending its complete report, to companies as defined in the Freight Rates Reduction Act of an aggregate amount in respect of the calendar year 1961 of $50 million, to be paid in instalments at such times and in accordance with such method of allocation as may be determined by the board of transport commissioners for Canada, as compensation to such companies for the maintenance of their rates on freight traffic at reduced levels as provided for in the said act.
So it covers the whole field. It covers the world. It covers in part the recommendation; in part salaries; in part reductions in freight rates. Again we have an example of the manner in which this government proceeds to deal with important matters of this character. We were also told we would have legislation in connection with these recommendations. That was a statement made repeatedly by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) during one of the debates of this house. We are still awaiting that legislation.
If the government had in mind the welfare of the railways and of the people of Canada it would, after this long period of time in which the report has been in its hands, have had legislation to deal with the situation as we find it. Under those circumstances, Mr. Speaker, there was every reason for the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to move this amendment, which we on this side of the house will support.

speechtext:
You had many opportunities to adopt such a bill if you had wanted to. But in keeping with your habit, you had one policy for the province of Quebec and another for the rest of the country. That is exactly what you have always done-try to divide and rule.
I have here, Mr. Speaker, an article of the newspaper Le Devoir of February 7, 1958, which I should like to quote in part:
The subject of bilingual cheques is not new. It has been discussed since the creation of family allowances at the end of the war. It is a known fact that the federal government had thought of issuing two sets of allowance cheques-bilingual cheques in the province of Quebec and English cheques for the other provinces in confederation.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that is evidence that the Liberals advocated two policies, one for Quebec and another for the rest of the country. It is a requirement of their political education. They always follow the same policy- divide and rule.
I continue:
French Canadians protested against such a rule which was inspired by the Quebec reserve thesis and requested bilingual cheques for the whole country in accordance with the spirit of the constitution. They soon referred to the fact that family allowance cheques were not the only cheques issued by the federal government, even if there were more of those and they asked that all cheques like currency be bilingual.

Financial Administration Act
The Conseil de Vie frangaise was our spokesman. On the eve of the 1953 election, it sent a delegation to Ottawa to submit a brief on bilingual cheques to Mr. Douglas Abbott.
The association made repeated representations to the different ministers of finance who came afterwards-i.e. Walter Harris and Donald Fleming. These representations were always well received but gave limited results.
In the commons, the independent member for Beauce supported these claims by introducing year after year a very well written bill that would have settled the question once and for all. His efforts were not useless since they forced the four federal political parties to accept the principle of a reform.
All that, Mr. Speaker, happened under the former Liberal government. That government could have given us bilingual cheques. But it did not.
Now that the Liberals are in the opposition, they demand that the government take steps they refused to take themselves.
I resume my reading of the article:
A quarter of a century ago, parliament and the nation had to deal with the question of bilingual currency. In those days as today, a Conservative government was in power in Ottawa and the Liberals who had been deaf to our demands, suddenly found themselves most zealous in the opposition.
Ever since the Liberal party has been confined to the cold regions of the opposition, they have felt a sudden outburst of patriotic and bilingual fever.
It still remains that they never did anything.
To further the expansion of bilingualism, the present Conservative government favours it not only in government buildings, but everywhere.
Indeed, everybody knows that the Department of Public Works is at present substituting bilingual traffic signs for unilingual ones.
The Liberals have been in power for 22 years and apparently, they never noticed this anomaly which the Conservative government is pleased to correct.
I would add that the Conservative government has no advice to take from the Liberal party in that respect and in many others.
Here is another proof of that. It was under a Conservative government led by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett that the currency minted in Canada was worded in French. Never before that had the Liberals dared take such a step. Never before had it occurred to them that there should be some French on our currency.
It is therefore R. B. Bennett who had the honour of having bank notes printed in French for the first time.
The purpose of the present resolution is to have negotiable instruments printed in both languages in Canada.
This motion should not have been introduced by a private member, because it calls for a spending of moneys and it rests with the government alone to introduce such a bill.
Be it as it may, hon. members may rest assured that, at the right moment, bilingual cheques shall be printed. And again a Conservative government will be the one to take steps in the interest of bilingualism.
For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I trust that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), when he deems advisable to do so, will give this country bilingual cheques, not only for the satisfaction of Conservative members, but for that of all the people of Canada, much to the regret of the Liberal members who, during the long years when they were in office, have not found time to do anything in that field.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased at this time to speak in strong and very sincere support of the bill now before us.
