speechtext:
My record on this subject is consistent. In spite of the interruptions I hear from the opposite side I would suggest that the record is a consistent one and I am very proud to be able to speak at this time in support of what I think is a very important piece of legislation. This is a bilingual country; it is a bicultural country and I think it behooves members of parliament to recognize this fact.
The hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot says that this government, or at least the Conservative party, will provide for bilingual cheques at the opportune time. I suggest that now is the opportune time. I ask why should we wait? For what reason are they delaying? I am certain that this measure would receive the unanimous support of this house now as it has on former occasions and that instead of talking it out a member of the cabinet should rise in his place and say that the government is prepared to accept the measure and to issue the proper instructions that instruments referred to in this measure be made bilingual.
It is easy for hon. members opposite to say, "Well, the Liberals should have done this. Why did they wait so long? They were here for 22 years and they failed to replace the plaques in the House of Commons by

substituting bilingual plaques". Well, if there have been mistakes in the past surely that is no excuse for continuing the mistake in this field. Why hark back to something that happened years ago when there are things that should be corrected now? To blame people for what happened over a 22-year period is certainly no excuse for talking on this bill at length, if that should be the position of hon. members opposite, and failing to bring it to a vote.
I am prepared to congratulate the government whenever it makes a move in this direction, but when criticism is justified I think that criticism should be made. Although for some years some of us have said that there should be placed within the employ of the government, that is within the civil service, at least two persons, one to instruct French speaking people in the English language and the other to instruct English speaking people in the French language, this has not been done. I do not know why this has not been done. Some members of parliament at any rate have been pressing it. There was a professor by the name of Edouard Pelo-quin who came to Ottawa periodically from Montreal one or two days a week to assist some of us in studying the French language. He was unable to continue his trips to Ottawa because of financial problems. The classes were not paying and he was losing money and was not able to finance these trips out of his own pocket. Some of us intervened with members of the government-

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to take part in this debate on Bill C-6, introduced by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska, in view of the fact that as early as 1959, I had placed my views on the record with regard to this matter.
In my humble view, it would not even be necessary to vote such a bill because, as the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) indicated a moment ago, the government could make this move without any legislative amendment. In fact, that was the view I expressed in 1959, and while I of course support the principle of this bill, I am still of the same opinion.
At that time, I argued that the problem could be settled through a government decision. As a matter of fact, I am sure the government will settle the matter in due course, despite what may be said to the contrary by our good friends in the opposition and even by members of the C.C.F. party, or the New party as it will soon be called, because as I understood the remarks

I referred a moment ago to the suggestion which he says was made years ago for the provision of courses for unilingual civil servants. I have not been a member of this house very long, but I do not think that suggestion was made so many years ago. I rather think it was made this year, when the new Civil Service Act came up, by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters).
I have no doubt that the teaching of English to French speaking civil servants and the teaching of French to English speaking civil servants would help solve the problem of bilingualism. However, it would not settle the whole problem which we considered when discussing that bill.
But to come back to the bill before us, with regard to the opportunity of enacting legislation to provide for the printing of negotiable instruments in both English and French, I think we did approve some bill to this effect before. It is, of course, another bill altogether and I do not want to deal with it, but it is more complete. I refer to Bill C-31 submitted by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) and which, to my mind, is more explicit than the one introduced by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska.
I shall not discuss it in detail, because I would be out of order since we are not allowed to deal with another bill when discussing a particular measure. However, I simply want to remind hon. members that I still think such legislation is unnecessary, and that the government can always take action in this respect. However, if the question were put, I say that I would still believe the other bill introduced by my colleague from Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm to be more adequate.

In any event, Mr. Speaker, I refer to the discussion which took place in 1959 on the matter, when the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska introduced an identical bill. At that time, I took part in the discussion in which various things were mentioned, like the constitutional guarantees with regard to the rights of the French and English languages and of bilingualism, guarantees which every year are more widely recognized, especially since the Conservative party came into power. It was referred to in some newspaper items and more particularly in an editorial printed in Le Droit, part of which I will read into today's record in a few moments, if I may do so, Mr. Speaker.
The various opinions expressed at that time were described as strange in some newspapers. I know that mine in particular was considered rather strange because it was said that although I was a French Canadian I was seeking to kill the bill. Such was not my intention, since I had already said that the government could implement such a plan without the necessity of making amendments to the act. An way, I feel that the attitude of our opponents who just took part in the discussion is not less strange, since now they are endeavouring to take credit for such legislation, which was introduced for the first time, as everybody knows, by the independent member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin). I am referring more particularly to the year 1956. It is true I was not in the house then, but I have looked into that matter. I should like to come back to the editorial quoted a moment ago by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot to the effect that when the Liberals were in power nothing was done to help pass the bill introduced by the former independent member for Beauce.
Not only that but when that bill came before the house in 1957, the Liberals resorted to all sorts of tricks and tactics behind the scenes. They even had statements in the press, trying to ridicule the hon. member for Beauce, Mr. Raoul Poulin, saying that he was seeking to bury his own bill, which was completely false, for if there was one who fought for bilingualism in this house, it is the former independent member for Beauce.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I wish first of all to place on the record a statement to the effect that I am in favour of the principle of this bill. We have had a very short debate on the subject of bilingual cheques. However, this subject under discussion has been before parliament on numerous occasions in the past. A similar bill was introduced by the same sponsor in 1959 and was debated in this house during the month of February of that year.
Although on the face of it the bill is a very simple one, the subject matter is of great importance. At the present time government cheques are issued in the English language in some parts of the country while other government cheques are issued in the French language. The debate in 1959 disclosed that, in addition to having English and French cheques, we have some cheques printed in both official languages. I believe the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Maloney) mentioned the fact that cheques of the St. Lawrence seaway authority and cheques of the C.B.C. were printed in both official languages. Hon. members who have spoken today, as have others in the past, suggested that legislation may not be necessary. I am one who supports that principle. However, debate on the principle is certainly necessary.
The explanatory note has not been mentioned today but for the purpose of the record I think some reference should be made thereto. It simply states that the purpose of the bill is to provide that cheques, drafts,
Financial Administration Act et cetera, and any other similar remittance of any department as defined in the Financial Administration Act shall be printed in both the English and the French languages. All hon. members and the public at large are familiar with the fact that currency under the Bank of Canada Act is bilingual. This has worked out satisfactorily and without any hardship or inconvenience. Bringing forth bilingual or bilingually printed cheques, et cetera would also be something easy to administer.
It was amusing to hon. members to hear the house leader of the C.C.F. speak in support of this bill. I believe all hon. members are generally in support of it. However, unlike the hon. member for Assiniboia, none of us is trying at this hour to appeal to the delegates who will soon be assembling at the convention in this city. Perhaps the delegates will listen to his words today and those from Quebec will be influenced by his statement.
I think the government as such is probably in favour of the principle because it was this government during this parliament that brought forth simultaneous translation of the debates of this house. Since then the record will show that this parliament has had more debate in the French language than has any parliament in recent years. In addition, it was this government that selected and appointed an outstanding Canadian of French origin to be Canada's first French speaking, native born governor general. Not long thereafter it was this government that supplied the funds in order to permit the C.B.C. to open the first French language television station east of Quebec. That station was opened a couple of years ago in Moncton, New Brunswick, a bilingual city supporting both the English culture and the French culture. After the opening of the television station this same government permitted the Canadian National Railways at great expense to construct a second microwave set-up in order to make it possible for the people of eastern New Brunswick and satellite areas to have daily live television emanating from Montreal owing to the existence of this second microwave facility.
Consequently, it should be very easy for hon. members on all sides, and particularly supporters of the government, to use their influence in order to convince the government of the importance of taking the necessary steps to implement the demand or request introduced by this bill. It may not require legislation to do so. However, the government must have an expression of the wishes of the people. I refer not only to the expression of the feeling of members of the House of Commons but editorial comment which may possibly follow this debate.

Mr. Speaker, we now have before us Bill C-121, the title of which reads as follows:
An act to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways system for the period from the 1st day of July, 1961 to the 30th day of June, 1962 and to authorize the guarantee by Her Majesty of certain securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railway Company.
What is the government asking of us by this bill? It is asking us to vote, for the benefit of the Canadian National Railways, a sum of $178,900,000. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), during the debate on second reading, moved the following amendment:
(Text):
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house declines to give second reading to a bill providing large sums for capital expenditures on the railway system while the house is not possessed of the identity of those, namely, the chairman and members of the board of directors, who will be responsible for the making of such expenditures."
(Translation):
The government is asking us to vote the sum of $178,900,000 for the Canadian National Railway Company; a crown corporation. Why? To refinance that crown corporation.
It seems to me that we have a right to know before agreeing to vote such an imposing amount, who are the people who will be appointed to administer the C.N.R. in the coming year. At this point, we are still in the dark. Perhaps the ministers do know. 

Perhaps the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) does know. But certainly parliament does not know.
Mr. Speaker, the comments made by the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Fournier) somehow surprised me. Incidentally, may I commend him for rising this afternoon to give his maiden speech in this house.
I am most surprised that a former minister of the crown from one of Canada's provinces should make the statement on constitutional theory he did this afternoon. He said, in fact, that it was up to the government to vote the necessary sums of money. I always thought that the members for the house were responsible for such control.
We are not only asked to give a cheque of considerable value to the C.N.R., but we are not even to be told in whose name that cheque will be made out. The company is, at present, administered by a president appointed from day to day whose term of office may expire overnight.
A bill was adopted on May 22 last, authorizing the government to increase the number of directors of the C.N.R. from seven to 12. There are, consequently, five directors to be appointed.
The minister told us then that he had in mind to appoint some fine Canadians. The Minister of Transport would surely not appoint a bad Canadian as director of the C.N.R. But one thing remains: these appointments are the responsibility of the government. Almost seven weeks have passed since that bill was carried. And it was said at that time that the bill would be put into effect as soon as proclamation would be given. What keeps the minister from going to his colleagues from the cabinet and telling them: "Now is the time to act; now is the time to proclaim this legislation". What keeps him from making his colleagues see reason? Would he, by chance, not have his word to say in the cabinet? Is this a one man government, who would appoint his own creatures to the board of directors of the C.N.R.?
We have been accused of repeating ourselves in this debate as well as in many others. But we are compelled to repeat ourselves because here is a government which refuses to take action when the time has come to act. Here is a government which refuses to take its responsibilities. The present government beats about the bush and waits until things have come to a crisis before settling problems. It is notorious for its confusion, irresponsibility and irresolution.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) has stated that we should look into other questions, for instance the trucking industry. I would like to point out that we will have an opportunity of discussing that point when the bill is before the committee. Right now, we are debating the amendment which has been moved. That point was raised by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets), amongst others. We will consider it when the bill is examined in committee and we will take that opportunity to ask the minister to what precise use those $178.9 million will be put.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to urge the minister once more to take his responsibilities and to see that Bill C-94 is proclaimed, so that the new C.N.R. directors may be appointed.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word or two on this matter. I am not of the opinion that we should refuse to make this money available to the C.N.R. because it is a maintenance grant in lieu of revenue and really is in the form of a loan to maintain the operations of the railway; yet I am in agreement with the fact that the government is not to be trusted in the making of appointments when it gets around to doing so. In parliament we have only certain methods of enabling the government to do what we wish it to do and one of them is by the voting of money to make these things possible.
We have seen what has happened in the case of some of the appointments made by the government. When these people were under pressure from the government they did things that they were not willing to do of their own free will. Not because the government has the responsibility for appointing these people and probably not because of the responsibility we expect them to have to parliament but because of the responsibility that we have to parliament itself, I believe it is exceedingly important that we must examine and on the basis of our knowledge be very cautious about appointments the government makes.
It is quite possible that Canadian National Railways is not being operated properly and will not be operated properly unless the right people are appointed to the board. On many occasions my colleague, the hon. member for Port Arthur, has shown his reluctance to support the chairman of the board. I was not a member of the railway committee this year but I am told that when he appeared before it his attitude had changed. He did make some suggestions. He did, so to speak, turn over a new leaf. I believe that
Canadian National Railways now it is the responsibility of the government to tell us, during the discussion of this bill, what their intention is in relation to his reappointment. The government should tell us whether they are going to appoint to the board people who are capable and qualified and who have the interests of the trucking industry at heart. It seems to me that trucking is becoming a greater and greater part of the transportation system known as Canadian National Railways, and it seems to me that the easiest way to make it impossible for us Canadians to afford a national railway system is to appoint people who are not qualified to speak for the trucking industry.
I believe, therefore, that we as members of parliament have a right to know who the directors are going to be. I believe we have the right to know whether they are being appointed for political reasons or whether they are being appointed because of a certain aptitude for the job they will be asked to do. Having in mind the remarks that have been made in the newspapers during the last two or three days about a board of directors, most of whom were appointed by this government in recent years, which made a decision and then for political reasons or under political direction made a complete about-face, I do not believe it is unfair for us to request this information. While it is not my intention to hinge our support of this measure on this request, I think it is important that, as members of parliament, we should give much closer attention to appointments to boards of directors of crown corporations. It seems to me there is a lack of good sense or good business judgment exhibited in the picking of directors for these companies. It would appear that in the case of one member of a board, to whom reference has been made in this house, the appointment depended entirely on the size of the contribution made to a candidate during the last election campaign.
I can see no reason why the minister cannot give us some indication of when these positions will be filled and who will fill them before we are called upon to pass this measure. This money will be used for the maintenance of the railway and it is necessary, therefore, to vote against the amendment which, in effect, would kill the loan that is to be made to Canadian National Railways. I do not believe our good judgment will permit us to pass on matters of this nature for much longer without being better informed than we are at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, the minister is of course introducing an annual bill; it is required every year. This year I think the annual expenditures are perhaps lower than we have experienced for some years. On the other hand we know that the committee on railways, air lines and shipping owned and controlled by the government was confronted not only with a capital budget that may be reduced but also with operating reports which indicate that last year the railway had an unprecedented deficit notwithstanding capital revision. The situation that concerns many of us is the fact that for 1961, despite the forecast of the Minister of Finance that we might have an increase in gross national product, we will still have a deficit of $64 million in this most important crown company.
In addition to that, only in the last portion of Bill No. C-121 do I find clauses in language unsimilar to that of those which we have met every year heretofore. There we have a very interesting and significant matter. I think this committee should concern itself with this matter because we have a proposal from the government to defer responsibility in two or three items upon which this house reached a decision ten years ago when there was another revision of the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways.
I think three clauses of this amending bill for 1691 are simply items of procrastination, and they are important items of procrastination. They refer to deferment of interest that might otherwise have been paid to the crown by this crown corporation on two or three items of concession given to the Candian National Railways ten years ago in 1951 in the revision of its capital structure. I hope the Minister of Finance will not be offended when I say this is rather typical of the procrastination in respect to decisions for which this government has been noted in recent times.
I indicated at the resolution stage that these capital revisions are of great consequence and I am not going to repeat myself in respect to that tonight. However, I indicated at that time that there had been write-offs to the extent of $700 million in 1951 and now a prospective write-off of an equivalent amount is to be postponed for one year. I think the minister should give us some indication when we are considering matters of this importance as to the direction in which the government might be leaning.
This government is now familiar with the testimony the chairman of the board of directors has given to the committee of this

house during its sittings this year. In view of the write-offs in 1937 and in 1951 of these gigantic amounts, in each case almost $700 million, I think the minister should explain why this government is not willing to face up this year to those obligations which were made evident by the statute some ten years ago at which time there was a revision following the royal commission. What is the reason behind the failure of this government to face up to its obligations rather than asking us by means of three new clauses in this annual bill to defer this obligation? What is the reason for the procrastination and indecision on the part of this government in carrying out its obligations made evident in at least two statutes? I refer, of course, to the Canadian National Railways Refunding Act revision of 1955, and of course the basic Canadian National Railways Refunding Act of 1951. The debts incurred as a result of those two revisions normally would require interest payments.
The main difficulty as I see it is that this government is nonchalantly evading its obligation to make a decision in respect to the management of the Canadian National Railways and is again asking for a deferment. This measure indicates procrastination and indecision on the part of the government in respect to this important matter of which it should obviously have been aware because of the statutes of some ten years ago to which I have referred. At that time it was known that the expiry date would be 1960 or 1961. Yet by these three clauses in this bill we are now being asked to give the government a blank cheque, further time and condonation in respect to its indecision and procrastination. I think the minister should indicate the reason for this inasmuch as it was known some ten years ago that this would be required either this year or last. It was known ten years ago that the chickens would come home to roost this year. I ask the minister to explain to this committee why he is now asking us to condone this indecision, because obviously there is to be no decision in this regard this year, despite the fact that he promised last year that there would be. I ask the minister why this committee should now give this government a postponement by adopting the subclauses of this bill, the effect of which will simply give the government another year to make up its mind.

We do not very often undertake capital revisions of the Canadian National system. The last one was to cover ten years. The next one may cover some years. Mr. Chairman, there is one point in connection with the auditor's report which I should like to draw to the attention of the minister. When the auditor was being questioned in the committee on railways, air lines and shipping I asked him certain questions about the trucking operations of the 90205-6-499
Canadian National Railways C.N.R. I should like to quote a portion of that discussion which is to be found at page 405 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping. I asked the following question:
In your work this year did you go into the operations and the accounts of these subsidiaries?
Mr. de Lalanne replied as follows:
Once these companies were actually 100 per cent or partially owned C.N.R. companies, I naturally considered it was part of my duty to satisfy myself with regard to whatever was being accumulated in the accounts of the C.N.R., for consolidation in these statements, and that the accounts were reasonably accurate, the same as I would in regard to hotels, telecommunications, and other things.
Now that I have looked at that statement in retrospect comparing it with the fact that Mr. Gordon indicated to us that Midland Superior, which is the largest of the trucking subsidiaries purchased by the C.N.R., is not included as actually being owned by the C.N.R., I would very much appreciate knowing whether Midland Superior came under audit in 1960. It has been suggested by other members that these trucking operations are in a peculiar position. I would certainly feel much better about that particular aspect of the Canadian National Railways trucking operation if we knew that it was being audited by the auditor for the Canadian National Railways. In view of the explanation given at page 405 of that report to which I have referred there is certainly some doubt in my mind that this is so. I felt this was a point worthy of bringing to the minister's attention for many reasons, not the least being because the president of the C.N.R. indicated that the profit from his particular company which apparently the C.N.R. does not own and does not show in its books was enough to balance the losses it incurred through the other trucking subsidiaries that it purchased. We have a most unusual situation here which I think is worthy of the minister's attention, and I should like to ask him to check with the auditor in this regard.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
since assuming office four years ago, the government has devoted much time and study to the problem of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. It has materially increased the return to the provinces from the existing tax-sharing arrangements by raising from 10 per cent to 13 per cent the standard rate on personal income tax; and by introducing the Atlantic Provinces Adjustment Grants, it has greatly broadened the fiscal aid element of federal assistance, and for the first time given full recognition to the special

financial disabilities of the Atlantic region. Although it has greatly improved the financial substance of the present arrangements, this government has recognized the weaknesses of the tax rental system which it inherited, both from the provincial and federal standpoint, and has become increasingly convinced of the need for a new approach which would give greater freedom and responsibility to the provincial governments, and which would be compatible with the constitution.
During the past year we have held three dominion-provincial conferences for the purpose of reaching agreement with the provinces on the form of the financial arrangements which should exist after the expiry of the present Federal-Provincial TaxSharing Arrangements Act on March 31, 1962. The first of those conferences was held July 25 to 27, 1960; the second, October 26 to 28, 1960 and the third February 23 to 24 of this year.
At the first of those dominion-provincial conferences, held July 25 to 27, 1960, the provinces presented their views on the form the new arrangements should take. Consideration of the financial substance of the provincial proposals made at that first conference will reveal the major weakness of the tax rental system. The provinces, like the federal government, have great and expanding responsibilities. In aggregate, the provincial proposals made at the July conference would have cost the federal treasury something in excess of $2 billion annually, an additional cost equal to more than one third of the total federal revenues for the fiscal year 1960-61. Under such circumstances it became increasingly evident that the tax rental system was unsound. It placed on the federal government the whole responsibility for levying the additional taxes to support large increases in provincial expenditures. The provincial governments assumed no responsibility for imposing the rented taxes on which they depended for revenues nor had they any freedom to amend the rates of these taxes in line with their current needs. Such a system was clearly destructive of provincial responsibility and initiative, and incompatible with the constitution which grants equal access to the federal and provincial governments in these fields of direct taxation.
Accordingly, at the October conference the Prime Minister suggested that the provinces might consider again imposing their own taxes on individual and corporate income, and their own succession duties at such rates as they judged appropriate in view of their needs for revenue. To make the

provincial re-entry into these tax fields practicable, the federal government was prepared to recommend to parliament that the federal tax rates in the three shared tax fields be reduced at the time of the termination of the present tax rental agreements, March 31, 1962, by the amount of the present effective standard rates, that is the so-called 13-9-50 formula.
I should explain that under section 2(3) of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act the standard individual income tax rate of 13 per cent is altered to compensate for any change in federal income tax rates from the rates in effect January 6, 1956. At the time of the October conference the effective rate determined in accordance with section 2(3) was 13.98353 per cent, or approximately 14 per cent. While offering a reduction in taxes equal to the standard rates the federal government was at the same time mindful of the need to support the revenue systems of the less well-to-do provinces and accordingly offered to recommend the continuation of a system of equalization.
On the basis of the discussion of the suggestions made at the October conference and further intensive study, the federal government advanced certain proposals at the dominion-provincial conference February 23 and 24 of this year. The Prime Minister's statement to the conference appears as an appendix to Hansard of February 28. As I stated in my budget speech of June 20, the main proposals were that the tax rental system be discontinued, that the provinces impose their own taxes and that a fair and more realistic system of equalization be introduced. At the same time the federal government undertook to reduce its income taxes to a larger extent than was suggested at the October conference. Instead of reducing the personal income tax by 14 per cent, which is the approximate effective standard rate at the present time, the federal government was prepared to recommend to parliament withdrawing from the personal income tax by 16 per cent in the first year of the agreements and an additional percentage point in each of the subsequent years so that in the final year the withdrawal would be 20 per cent.
This additional tax room was offered to the provinces in the personal income tax rather than in the corporation income tax quite deliberately and for good reasons: first, because of the steadier and more rapid growth of personal income tax yields the personal income tax is a more satisfactory revenue source from a provincial standpoint; second, many corporations operate on a national scale and corporation profits are therefore generally regarded as more appropriate 90205-6-499J
Dominion-Provincial Relations for taxation by the federal government; third, the present provincial share of corporation income taxes is 9 percentage points on corporate taxable income, or about 22 per cent to 23 per cent of total corporation income taxes, so that it is reasonable to increase the provincial share of personal income tax before making any adjustment with respect to corporation income taxes.
In short, the provinces would reassume their constitutional rights and responsibilities to impose and vary their tax levies as they saw fit. At the same time in the interests of administrative simplicity and uniformity and in order to save the provinces the expense of setting up tax collection machinery of their own, the federal government was prepared to collect the provincial personal income and corporation income taxes free of charge provided the provincial tax base was identical with the federal tax base at all times. It was explained that this offer could not be extended to the estate tax since the provinces do not have the constitutional power to levy an estate tax on the federal basis. Accordingly, the federal offer in respect of the estate tax was that any province not levying succession duties would receive half the yield of the federal estate tax while an abatement of 50 per cent of the federal estate tax would be granted as at present to provinces levying their own succession duties.
The proposals presented by the Prime Minister to the conference on February 23 and 24 were discussed at that conference and subsequently received intensive consideration and re-examination by federal and provincial officials at two meetings of the Continuing Committee on Fiscal and Economic Matters. In the light of this further study, the proposals were re-examined by the federal government and a letter was written to the provincial premiers by the Prime Minister on June 16 of this year. This letter was tabled in this house and appears in Hansard of June 19.
As the present resolution indicates, the proposal of a system of tax collection agreements to replace the tax rental agreements is a central part of the new approach and is provided for in the bill which I shall introduce. Obviously a system which gives the provinces the right to vary the rates of taxation without imposing on them the administrative burden of collecting the taxes has great advantages for them. It restores the necessary flexibility to the provincial tax system, enabling the provinces to meet increased needs for revenue not only from such sources as the sales tax, the gasoline tax and motor vehicle revenues but from the direct taxes on income which have for the past 20 years been controlled by agreement. The counterpart of

Dominion-Provincial Relations this freedom and flexibility is the independence and responsibility of the provinces. There can be no question that in a healthy federal state in which the goal should be enlightened co-operation rather than centralization, it will be better for the provinces to face up to their responsibilities of levying taxes for provincial purposes in the tax fields which were assigned to them by the constitution.
I referred in my budget speech to the fact that replacing the tax rental agreements by tax collection agreements would also have advantages from the federal standpoint. The provinces will be in the position of having to assess realistically their new proposals for expenditure in the light of their revenue potential rather than placing increasing pressure on the federal government. The federal budget will no longer be inflated by taxation which can and should be imposed at the provincial level. I estimate that for the first year of the new arrangements the adoption of a tax collection system will remove more than $300 million from the federal budget.
I have referred to the fact that the federal government was prepared to recommend to parliament certain reductions in the rates of the federal income tax in order to permit the re-entry of the provincial governments into these fields. The amount of these reductions was set forth in my budget speech.

When this government took office in 1957 the standard rates under the tax rental agreements were 10-9-50, that is to say, the provinces received 10 per cent of the personal income tax collections, 9 percentage points on the taxable income of corporations and 50 per cent of the succession duty or estate tax. In 1958 this government introduced legislation increasing the provincial share of the personal income tax from 10 to 13 per cent. With the permission of the house I should like to place on Hansard at this point table No. 1 which indicates the increase in provincial revenue which resulted from this increase of 3 percentage points in the standard rate of individual income tax. May I have that leave, Mr. Chairman?

The table indicates that the total value of these payments and abatements has more than doubled in the short space of five years-from $689.4 million in 1956-57 to $1,470.1 million in 1961-62.
As I mentioned earlier, the proposal to offer tax collection agreements and to increase the share of the personal income tax available to the provinces was accompanied by a proposal for an improved system of equalization and larger grants to the Atlantic provinces. As the resolution indicates, provision is made for equalization payments, payments to the Atlantic provinces, stabilization payments, and payments of a special grant of $8 million per annum to Newfoundland.
Under the present arrangements equalization is based on the per capita yield from the three standard taxes, that is, from the personal income tax, corporation income tax and succession duties at the standard rates of 13-9-50 in the two provinces which have the highest per capita yield. There are two fundamental weaknesses in this formula. The first is that equalization to the per capita yield in the two provinces with the highest yield is not realistic. The second is that by limiting the equalization formula to the three standard taxes no account is taken of wide variation in the revenues from other provincial sources. Equalization based on standard tax yields in the top two provinces led in some instances to larger payments than could be defended on the basis of fiscal need. At the same time it took no account of variations in fiscal capacity due to differences in other revenue sources.
It was with these considerations in mind that the government decided to propose an equalization formula based on the national average yields of standard taxes plus 50 per cent of the natural resource revenues. I should like at this point to refer to two tables which were presented to the dominion-provincial conference of February 23-24 of this year and which appear as an appendix to Hansard of March 7, 1961, in order to illustrate the effect of the new proposals. The first is a table showing natural resource revenue for the years 1956, 1957 and 1958, and the second is a table which illustrates the effect of including provincial natural resource revenue in the equalization formula. It will be seen from examination of the first table that there is an extremely wide variation in the amount of natural resource revenue per capita in the provinces, ranging from a low of 18 cents per capita for the three year average in Prince Edward Island to a high of $112.17 per capita in Alberta. The national average is $16.62 per capita. It was because of this extreme variation that it was decided that the inclusion
of some portion of natural resource revenue in the equalization formula would produce a much better indication of fiscal need. It was decided therefore to include only 50 per cent of the average natural resource revenue on the ground that this would allow for some variation in the different rates of taxation in the provinces while at the same time not discouraging the provinces from using this revenue source.
The other element in the equalization formula consists of the standard taxes. For purposes of the equalization formula, the standard rates will be the rates by which the federal government withdraws from the standard tax fields, that is, 16-9-50 in the first year, 17-9-50 in the second year, 18-9-50 in the third year, 19-9-50 in the fourth year, and 20-9-50 in the fifth and final year of the new period. This means that the basis of the equalization payments will rise throughout the period as the federal government leaves increasing room in the personal income tax field for the provinces. The national average per capita yield of the standard taxes for any year plus 50 per cent of national average per capita return from natural resources for the average of the three preceding years will thus constitute the level below which no province can fall.
In addition, two equalization guarantees are provided. First, for provinces below the national average in the yield of standard taxes and 50 per cent of natural resource revenue, the equalization will never be less than enough to make them at least as well off as they would have been under a projection of the present arrangements. Second, for no province will the equalization payments ever be less than enough to bring its total receipts under the new arrangements up to the level of its total receipts in the final year of the old arrangements or in the average of the last two years of the old arrangements, whichever is the greater. The equalization provisions are applicable to all provinces whether or not they enter into tax collection agreements with the government of Canada.
At this point, with the permission of the house, I should like to place on Hansard table No. 3 containing a hypothetical illustration of how the equalization formula would apply to the year 1962-63 on certain assumptions.

I should point out that the figures in this hypothetical illustration differ somewhat from those presented at the February conference and tabled in Hansard of March 7, 1961, because they are based on more up to date estimates.
The above table gives a comparison between the estimated amount the provinces would have received under a projection of the arrangements in effect when this government took office four years ago when the standard rates were 10-9-50 and their estimated receipts under the new arrangements proposed. It will be seen from this table that in aggregate the provinces will be $127.5 million better off under the proposed arrangements than they would have been under the arrangements in effect four years ago. This is the estimated benefit in the first year of the proposed arrangements. This benefit will increase materially in subsequent years as the federal income tax withdrawal increases from 16 per cent to 20 per cent.
The resolution also refers to increased grants to the Atlantic provinces, bringing the total of these grants from $25 million in each of the last four years to $35 million for each of the five years in the next period. This special and separate recognition of the fiscal problems of the Atlantic region was initiated by this government and has been widely acclaimed, not only in the Atlantic region. It complements the improved equalization formula. The decision to increase these grants by 40 per cent for the next five year period is a further indication of the emphasis which this government wishes to put upon the need for placing all regions of Canada in a position to supply essential services without resorting to unduly burdensome levels of taxation.
The resolution also indicates that the bill will provide for an additional payment of $8 million per annum to the province of Newfoundland for each of the five years of the new period. This is in recognition of the special fiscal need of the province of Newfoundland.
The over-all effect of the new equalization formula taken together with the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants and the special payment of $8 million per annum to Newfoundland will be a greater emphasis on fiscal need. I should like to illustrate this fact by making certain comparisons. In 1957-58, the first year of the present tax rental arrangements, the total equalization payments of $136.0 million were distributed as follows: Newfoundland, 8.5 per cent; Prince Edward Island, 2.2 per cent; Nova Scotia, 12.8 per cent; New Brunswick, 6.4 per cent;

Quebec, 31.7 per cent; Ontario, nil; Manitoba, 10.2 per cent; Saskatchewan, 14.1 per cent; Alberta, 10.8 per cent; and British Columbia, 3.3 per cent.
In the first year of the new proposals the estimated total of fiscal aid including equalization, Atlantic provinces grants and the special grant of $8 million to Newfoundland will be $216.7 million and will be distributed as follows: Newfoundland, 15.2 per cent; Prince Edward Island, 3.2 per cent; Nova Scotia, 13.8 per cent; New Brunswick, 11.9 per cent; Quebec, 33.4 per cent; Ontario, nil; Manitoba, 5.9 per cent; Saskatchewan, 10.3 per cent; Alberta, 5.8 per cent; and British Columbia, 0.5 per cent. Thus the share of these greatly increased fiscal aid payments going to the Atlantic region will have risen from 29.9 per cent to 44.1 per cent. By the end of the five year period of the new proposals the share going to the Atlantic region will be over 50 per cent, provided rates of growth are not greater in the Atlantic region than elsewhere in Canada. Thus the new formula gives full recognition to the principle of equalization and fiscal need which this government has always maintained to be essential. At the same time the federal treasury will be saved the expense of paying equalization on an unrealistic basis and unsupported by fiscal need.
Under the present tax rental agreements certain stabilization provisions were included to protect the provinces against an undue decline in the revenue from the standard taxes and equalization. It can be argued that it is not the federal government's responsibility under tax collection agreements to protect the provinces from declines in the yield of their own taxes. It was evident, however, during the course of the discussions, that the provinces attached considerable importance to the stabilization provisions of previous agreements. Under the existing arrangements, the stabilization provisions ensure that a province will not receive less in any year from standard taxes, equalization, and stabilization than 95 per cent of the total it received in the average of the two preceding years. It was decided as a concession to the provinces to continue this provision so that even under tax collection arrangements all provinces, including those which do not enter into collection agreements, will be protected from an inordinate decline in the revenues from the standard taxes and equalization.
Reference is made in the resolution to the fact that the bill will provide for advance payments in respect of the taxes collected under the tax collection agreements with the provinces. The details of the tax collection agreements will have to be worked out in the course of the succeeding months. However, it

has been evident from the discussions to date that some of the provinces will wish the tax collection payments to provide for an even flow of revenue throughout each fiscal period as is provided under the present tax rental agreements. Therefore it is necessary to provide authority for the federal government to pay out money to the provinces on an estimated basis pending the final determination of the amounts of provincial tax assessed year by year.
I wish at this time to refer to three other matters which are not included in the bill but which may nevertheless be regarded as part of the proposed fiscal arrangements for the provinces for the period after March 31, 1962.
Under the 1947 and 1952 Tax Eental Agreements Acts provision was made for paying to the provinces half of the federal income tax collected from certain public utility corporations whose main business is the distribution or generation for distribution to the public of electrical energy, gas or steam in respect of income of the corporation derived from the said distribution or generation. This sharing has been continued on a year to year basis since then and has been provided for in the estimates. It was evident from the discussions at the conferences that most of the provinces attach great importance to the continuation of this arrangement. As a concession to the representations made by the provinces, the government proposes to give the assurance that this sharing will be continued throughout the period of the next agreements, that is, for the next five years up to and including the fiscal year 1966-67.
A second matter which will be dealt with outside the provisions of the bill is the matter of a co-operative approach toward the taxation of the forest industry. Under the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, provincial taxes on the income from logging operations are specifically excluded from the corporation taxes which a province must refrain from levying in order to enter into a tax rental agreement with the government of Canada. Taxes on logging profits are imposed in two provinces, Ontario and British Columbia, and although these taxes are deductible as expenses in computing federal income tax, the result has been that in these provinces the forest industry bears somewhat higher income taxes than other industries. It was because of the government's concern with this situation that the Prime Minister made the following statement in his letter of June 16, 1961 to the provincial premiers:
At the conference I stated that the federal government was prepared to consider certain concessions in connection with the taxation of the forest industry if the provinces were willing also to make some concessions. It has been conceded
Dominion-Provincial Relations that because the logging profits tax is levied in addition to the corporation income tax, the forest industry bears a greater tax burden than other industries. The possibilities of lessening the burden of taxation on the forest industry have been discussed at the official level. One of the possibilities discussed was that a tax credit, shared between a province and Canada, might be granted to the industry.
Before this can be done some further technical discussions will be required to reach agreement on the definition of logging income which will be subject to tax and accepted for the purpose of this tax credit. Subject to reaching agreement on this matter of the definition of logging income, the federal government is prepared as a means of relieving the tax burden on the forest industry to offer a tax credit equal to two thirds of the logging tax up to a maximum rate of 10 per cent, provided the province gives a tax credit equal to the remaining one third of such logging tax.
A third matter has been under discussion with the provinces for some time and that is the application of provincial sales taxes to federal agencies and corporations. Similar agencies and corporations at the provincial level have been subject to federal sales and excise taxes and it has been the contention of the provinces that federal agencies should be placed in the same position. At the February conference the Prime Minister made the following statement concerning this matter:
We have given further thought to the means of achieving reciprocity of treatment in the position of provincial crown corporations and agencies under federal sales and excise taxes and the position of federal corporations and agencies under provincial direct taxes on purchases. We are prepared to waive federal immunity from taxation and instruct federal corporations and agencies to pay provincial purchase taxes and other similar taxes, on the understanding that provincial corporations and agencies will be subject to federal sales and excise taxes. We think that this is an equitable arrangement, being in accordance with the general principles followed in regard to the payment of federal taxes on purchases by federal departments. We think it is better than reciprocal exemptions as an administrative and accounting arrangement, preserving as it will a fairer relationship between crown corporations and agencies in general and private businesses.
We are proceeding with the preparation of a list of federal agencies and corporations which would be subject to provincial sales taxes and any necessary legislation providing for such payment of taxes will be introduced to take effect April 1 next year.
I have now explained the main features of the bill as provided for in the resolution and have dealt with certain ancillary matters which are part of the fiscal arrangements. The provisions of the bill will reaffirm and strengthen the principle that equalization payments must take full account of fiscal need and at the same time enable the provinces to exercise their constitutional rights of taxation. The government is convinced that the new arrangements provided for under the bill

Dominion-Provincial Relations will be the basis for a sound partnership between the provinces and the federal government and will usher in a new era of cooperation on more equal terms.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
In what some of us still persist in hoping are the dying hours of this session which began last November the minister has put before the committee a resolution dealing with a subject which is almost as important as any subject can be in a federal state, namely the fiscal and financial relationships between the provinces and the central government. Our whole history shows the importance of this matter in national development, unity and strength. If that development in our federal society cannot proceed in a way which provides for the maintenance of a reasonably balanced level of essential services throughout the country so that there will not be in this federation underdeveloped areas in that sense, our history shows that the federation cannot be strong. Our history also shows that this consideration puts an obligation on the federal government to assist, through fiscal aid and financial aid, those provinces which are not as fortunate as others in their resources and because of that fact have not access to as much financial resources as have some of the more fortunate and richer provinces. That is the basis on which the federal government has helped the provinces ever since 1867.
In his statement the minister said that the principle in the relations between the provinces and the federal government in this field, and I would add in every other field, must be one of enlightened co-operation rather than centralization. Of course, Mr. Chairman, we all agree with that statement. We on this side will consider the application of this formula in that light, namely whether it implements the principle of enlightened cooperation; whether it is fair in its impact on the poorer provinces; and above all, whether it implements in a fair and equitable way the principle to which we on this side have always attached so much importance, namely the principle of equalization. The minister spoke for some time, Mr. Chairman, and we will examine with great care what he has said. Especially will we examine the statistical tables he has placed on the record. I thought some of the minister's arguments and some of his statements, and especially his passion now for the principle of equalization, were a little disingenuous in the light of the past history of the attitude of his party to this matter. I also noticed that, among the tables which the minister inserted into the record, he did not include, or at least I did not gather that he did so, one which we would certainly like to see included, namely a table 
which would show what the continuation of the present arrangement would mean to the provinces in comparison with the application of the new formula.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is on record in one of the earlier tables.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As I say, we will study these tables with interest. I have not had much chance tonight to do that. We will have something to say about these tables and we shall also be glad indeed to put on Hansard a few tables of our own, as our interpretation of the application of this new formula is certainly not that which has been given to us tonight by the minister. In any event, this new formula or this new deal embodied in this resolution on which a bill will be based is apparently the result of four years' consideration given to this matter by the federal government. This is the final outcome of the promises made by the Prime Minister and his colleagues in the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958 when they told the provinces there would be a new deal which would be acceptable to all the provinces and welcomed by them. We remember particularly the statements made by the Prime Minister in Ontario and the reaction of those statements by the premier of Ontario. We also remember the amount which the premier of Ontario said would be fair to that province under the new deal which he assumed the new government would give him and on the strength of which he begged the people of Ontario to "follow John".
That amount was $100 million.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That amount was $100 million. They have not followed John into $100 million for Ontario but they followed him into a sales tax for Ontario.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If these proposals which the minister has put before the committee tonight carry out all these desirable principles which the minister has mentioned such as equalization, enlightened co-operation, greater assistance to the provinces and greater recognition of provincial fiscal needs, it is a strange thing that these proposals have not been accepted with enthusiasm by all the provinces.
That has not happened. Most of the provinces have been dissatisfied with the deal which has been put before them. Some provinces, especially the less rich provinces, are complaining about the inadequacy of this formula which is a result of four years' consideration by this government and which was

to put the fiscal relations of the provinces and the federal government on a new and more satisfactory basis.
The resolution contains these words:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize tax collection agreements with the governments of the provinces-
We will have something to say about these agreements:
-and to provide that the minister may pay to a province, out of the consolidated revenue fund, in respect of any fiscal year in the period commencing on the 1st day of April, 1962 and ending on the 31st day of March, 1967,
(a) a tax equalization payment;
The minister had a great deal to say this evening about this principle of equalization and the way this formula was implementing it in a way which would strengthen rather than weaken the principle. We claim, and we will be able to produce evidence to support the claim, that the equalization formula weakens rather than strengthens the principle. In any event, the principle itself is not so important as the base on which the principle is applied. For the minister to argue that by altering the base from the top two provinces to the national average strengthens rather than weakens the principle is very, very difficult for us on this side of the house to understand. We would like the minister in the course of this discussion to tell us how this equalization payment under the new formula will actually affect the various individual provinces. I am not sure whether the tables the minister introduced tonight deal with that matter, but perhaps he will deal with it before the debate is over.
The government has claimed, and the minister has repeated the claim this evening, that these new tax collection agreements represent a return to the spirit of the constitution and this gives back to the provinces their complete rights in the field of direct taxation. The minister claims that this represents, in that sense, a very great advance over the tax rental agreement formula. Of course that claim, if I may use the minister's favourite word, is nonsense. Under the present system which has been applied since 1957 three options were offered to the provinces. They could levy and collect their taxes at whatever rates they wished to determine themselves. They have always had that option. They could simply rent the three direct tax fields or they could levy those taxes, and the federal government was willing to collect them provided the provincial rates did not exceed the standard rates. Up to the present, then, the provinces have had these three options. Nobody forced them into the tax rental agreement field. They had the other options. Under the new formula the rental option would
Business of the House cease to be available and the federal government would be willing to collect provincial taxes at any rates.
While this last change-the minister went to some pains to illustrate this point this evening-may be an improvement for certain of the richer provinces, it can hardly be described as a revolutionary change. The minister called it-and I am paraphrasing what he said-a sort of introduction of the idea of flexibility. He said this provides more flexibility in these areas. But this new arrangement may very well lead to the tax jungle of the 1930's. Moreover, to the extent that the provinces will have to depend on additional direct taxes without equalization for their financing, great regional inequalities will arise because for most of the provinces equalization is a very important source of revenue. We claim that the principle of equalization and the application of that principle in the new formula will react to the disadvantage of the poorer provinces. Indeed the provinces themselves have already pointed that out to the minister. They seem singularly ungrateful for this new deal which according to the minister is going to mean so much to them.
Therefore we on this side of the house claim that the equalization principle is weakened under this new formula and we will produce evidence to support that contention. We claim that the new proposal is much more a return to the tax jungle and the inequalities of the 1930's than even the 1867 arrangement which embodied a large element of equalization.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it 10.30.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
What are the latest figures under the National Housing Act for (a) housing (b) assistance on municipal sewage projects (c) loans for university residences, during 1961?
Answer by: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minisier of Public Works):
(a)	In June, housing starts in urban centres numbering 10,644 dwelling units were at the highest level since November, 1959, and represented an increase of 22.3 per cent over June, 1960.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a short statement to make concerning Canada's special commonwealth African aid program.
The house will be interested to know that agreement has been reached for an aerial mapping project to be undertaken in Nigeria as a part of our assistance program. This project, which is the first Canadian capital project in Nigeria since that country attained independence, will include an aerial survey and topographical mapping of approximately 28,000 square miles. It is expected that the maps which will result from this project will greatly facilitate the economic development of Nigeria. The cost of the entire project is estimated at $1,350,000. It will be undertaken by a Canadian company over a period of two or three years, subject to the appropriation of the necessary funds by parliament.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EXTENSION OF FISHING LIMIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as members of the house will recall, Canada made intensive efforts both before and during the 1960 conference on the law of the sea to bring about international agreement on the breadth of the territorial sea and contiguous

Income Tax Act
zone. The failure of the conference has not, however, meant the abandonment of our interest or our efforts in this field. speechtext:

On subclause 3.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the tax advantages accorded to such a plan depend upon registration. Therefore they run from the date of registration, and that is why this subclause has been included.

Mr. Chairman, that answer is not very illuminating, if I may say so. The language of the subclause says:
Where a profit sharing plan is accepted by the minister for registration as a deferred profit sharing plan, the plan shall be deemed to have become registered as a deferred profit sharing plan
(a)	on the date the application for registration of the plan was made, or
(b)	where in the application for registration a later date is specified as the date upon which the plan is to commence as a deferred profit sharing plan, on that date.
Does that mean that if an application is not considered for a considerable period of time, as might very well be the case while an investigation was being carried on, it would in fact be considered to be in force from the very date on which the application was received by the Minister of National Revenue?

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, unless the application indicated that the plan was to come into effect at some date later than the date of application.

On subclause 5.
Mr. Chairman, the explanation to subclause 5 does not leap to the eye. No doubt the minister can explain it very simply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should have thought this was plain. This clause states that for a period during which

a plan is a deferred profit sharing plan, the plan shall be deemed, for the purposes of the act, not to be an employees' profit sharing plan. There is a difference between an employees' profit sharing plan and a deferred profit sharing plan. The definitions of this clause under consideration are included in subclause 1.
Subclause 5 agreed to.
On subclause 6.
Mr. Chairman, perhaps the minister ought to give us some explanation in respect to paragraph (b) of subclause 6.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I should add to my last observation that employees' profit sharing plans are defined in section 79, subsection 1 of the act.
I see; that is not in this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a definition in this bill of profit sharing plans as well as a definition of deferred profit sharing plan, but there is a definition in the act now in respect to employees' profit sharing plans.

Mr. Chairman, I must confess that this did puzzle me a little bit and, of course, it is for the reason the minister gave to the committee last night, that I do not have that familiarity with the act that he has. It did seem to me that they were both employees' profit sharing plans but one was deferred. I was a little puzzled by the language. I can see that one is an immediate profit sharing plan while the other is a deferred one, if I might put it that way. Perhaps "immediate" would not be the right word to use. Perhaps it is an annual disbursement profit sharing plan or something of that sort; is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, not necessarily. If the hon. member will have regard to the section of the act he will readily see the difference. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told since 1954.

My hon. friend from
Kenora-Rainy River got up before I had
Income Tax Act
completed the question I wanted to ask about this deferred profit sharing plan and the employees' profit sharing plan. In his answer the minister rather gave the impression, and the language in subclause 5 does give the impression, that a deferred profit sharing plan is not an employees' profit sharing plan; that is, my understanding is that a deferred profit sharing plan is a plan for profit sharing by employees only. Is that not correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, employees in the broad sense of the word. It might of course include officers of the company.

I think the minister will see where my difficulty lies, in that I had not read the definition in the act itself. It does seem to me there ought to be a little more clarity in the definition to draw a distinction between a deferred profit sharing plan and an employees' profit sharing plan. It seems to me that you need another word that is the antithesis of "deferred" in there, because both plans relate only to employees. Does the minister not think there might be defective draftsmanship there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, sir.
Would the minister give consideration to the possibility that there might be, and there might be an occasion for misunderstanding, and perhaps have it reviewed further?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I did refer to that last evening in reviewing the clause and pointing out the exemption that exists. Income Tax Act

This is, of course, one of the measures that is calculated by the government, I suppose-perhaps not to direct; that is far too strong a word-but to suggest to Canadians who have savings plans of one kind or another that it would be desirable for them to invest those savings in Canada. That is a position that I do not quarrel with, a position that Mr. Coyne, of course, has been taking for a long time, and that the government appeared to accept from him in the baby budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The government did not accept it from Mr. Coyne in the supplementary budget or anywhere else.

We will let the public judge that and they are making a judgment, I might add; but that perhaps, sir, is slightly irrelevant to the discussion here. I may say that personally I think it is desirable, notwithstanding the fact that this government proclaims that it is a great free enterprise government, that where these tax incentives and tax advantages are given they should be used in order to encourage, to provide incentives for people to invest in their own country. The clause certainly commends itself to me as I would imagine it does to most other members of the house; but it did seem to me, sir, that perhaps the government was hiding its light under a bushel, and hiding the source of its light under a bushel.

Mr. Chairman, in the submission of the Canadian chamber of commerce to the minister in April, 1961 they reported to him that they had examined last year's Bill C-84, and the executive council went on record as endorsing the postponement of tax on members of deferred profit sharing plans until such times as payments were actually received. speechtext: The gist of it, Mr. Chairman, is completely set forth in the explanatory note. On subclause 9.
The minister might give us an explanation of this subclause.

speechtext:

provided under this legislation. Upon which under the law in the past he has paid tax.

I take it, then, that there is no tax paid on capital gains in respect of any of these funds?

And no credit is given for capital loss.
