speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We had that last night, Mr. Chairman. If the hon. member will look back at subclause 2(c) he will find that the plan must not provide that any part of the funds in the trust governed by the plan may be invested in notes, bonds, debentures, or similar obligations of (1) an employer by whom payments are made in trust to a trustee under the plan for the benefit of beneficiaries thereunder, or (2) a corporation with whom that employer does not deal at arm's length.

In other words it is perfectly clear that under no circumstances will one of these plans be recognized if any part of the funds in it is used in any fashion as capital or as a loan to the company that has made the profits. Perhaps the minister could explain that. That is what it seems to me to be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He can invest in shares of the company.
Could the whole amount be invested in shares of the company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. There is no limit on the shareholdings of the company.
I wish to pursue that a little further. I understood from what the minister said that these funds could not be invested in any way in the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The reference is to notes, bonds, debentures or similar obligations. Capital stock is not an obligation.

I quite appreciate that, but that raises this question. Why should there be this distinct prohibition on fixed interest obligations and things of that sort? Why should it be competent to invest in something that may or may not produce a profit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A great many of these plans are designed to encourage the employees to acquire a share of the stock ownership of the company that is the employer.
What fear is there of having them invest in the other obligations of the company? Is this a treasury provision? What does the treasury fear may happen?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We were on this subject last night, Mr. Chairman. It is in kind with various other provisions of the act. If such provisions were not written into the act here and elsewhere it would be possible for a taxpayer who has obtained a tax advantage under given circumstances to get his money back by the appearance of a loan. We dealt with this subject last evening. It is the same situation, and the same reason applies.

It would appear to me to be equally easy, if the company had an authorized capital which had not all been subscribed, for the fund to subscribe to the additional stock and the company thereby to get back the money just as effectively and indeed more effectively, because there would be no obligation to pay any interest on it. That would appear to me to be as easy or easier than would be the case with a loan or bonds or debentures. To my simple mind there does not appear to be much valid reason in what the minister said about getting back the money. There may be some other reason, as indeed I am sure there must be. I am sure this was not included simply to make the bill more complicated.
What precisely is the concern? When all is said and done I assume that the company,

unless it went broke and defaulted, would have to pay back this amount and would have to pay interest in the meantime. There does not seem to be any possible loss to the treasury because of this provision. It would appear to me that it must be included in order, in some way, to protect the funds. If it is included to avoid a loss to the treasury I wish the minister would explain how a loss to the treasury could occur.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have endeavoured to do that, Mr. Chairman. I think the hon. member does not appreciate the difference between the acquisition of stock in a company which carries with it a share of ownership in the company and the distribution or recovery by the company of money through the issuance of what would appear to be debentures, notes or bonds thus recovering the benefit of money that has been contributed to the fund by the employer and for which he has received a tax deduction. This is fully understood by the business community.
Well, Mr. Chairman, no doubt it is understood by the business community but I am a member of parliament, just like everyone else in this chamber.
Not quite like anyone else in this chamber.

The mere fact that it is understood by the business community does not justify the failure of the minister to give a comprehensive reason. I put this question to the minister. Let us suppose that company A which has one of these deferred profit sharing plans borrows $10,000 from the Bank of Montreal at the same rate of interest as company B, which borrows a similar sum from the trustee of the profit sharing plan. Is not the relationship of both those loans to the treasury precisely the same? What tax advantage would company B receive through borrowing from the trustee over what company A would receive as a result of borrowing from the Bank of Montreal at the same rate of interest? If that were explained to me I think I would see the point, but at the moment I fail to see that the source of funds makes any difference as far as the treasury is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It makes a great deal of difference if you are opening the door to all kinds of transactions under which the employer is simply recovering his money and handing over what may be no more than a piece of paper, a note. This would open the door to all kinds of devices that could defeat the purposes of the legislation.
90205-6-496
Income Tax Act

As far as I can make out, what the minister is now saying is that this has nothing at all to do with revenue and nothing to do with the treasury. This represents an attempt to protect these funds from abuse, to protect the participants in the funds from unscrupulous employers who might borrow the money, pay no interest on it and never pay it back. Surely that would be a felony. It does not seem to me that if the employer borrows some money and pays the same rate of interest he would pay through the Bank of Montreal, there can be any possible difference between the two transactions except that you might say the employer is himself both the lender and the borrower, which is perhaps not a desirable situation to have from the point of view of the solvency of the fund. But from the point of view of the treasury, which the minister implied was the reason for this, I cannot get through my head what conceivable difference there would be in the two sets of circumstances. It seems to me we have not received an adequate explanation.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Subclause agreed to.
On subclause 13.
Mr. Chairman, before this subclause passes I feel the minister should give us-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is perfectly obvious to any hon. member who will read this subclause that it deals with the circumstances under which the minister may revoke the registration of a deferred profit sharing plan. It sets out the circumstances under which he may do so.

Now that the minister has anticipated what he thought would be my question, Mr. Chairman, I shall put to him the question I wished to have him answer. Even I can read the word "revocation" and even I know what it means. This subclause raises the question which as yet has not been answered, as to how the minister is going to find out when revocation should take place. This is a great vacuum, if I may express it in that way, in this whole scheme.
Provisions are laid down for the registration of these schemes and provision is made for revoking them if the conditions are not fulfilled, but no evidence has been given to us relating to policing and no provision appears to have been made for any form of policing of the schemes. That seems to me to be a serious lack and imperfection in the whole scheme when we are embarking on a savings plan of this kind. It is true, as the minister has said, that these are not employee savings, but this represents a scheme whereby the

Income Tax Act
government in future is going to permit profit sharing, which is now a current annual thing, to be deferred to create a property and estate which the employee may enjoy in his old age. If that is to be done under conditions laid down by this parliament, because many people are not able to protect themselves very well in these matters we should know precisely how these schemes are going to be policed and how effective that policing will be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The statute does not put any limitations in the way in which information may come to the minister on which he may see fit to act to revoke the registration of a plan. As to what is to be involved in the detailed administration, there is really nothing I can usefully add to what I said last night. We spent considerable time on this matter last evening, and I discussed this subclause in relation to other subclauses bearing on the same subject.

I recognize at once, Mr. Chairman, that what the minister says is quite true. However, I had hoped that after reflecting on this overnight the minister would come to the conclusion that the information he gave us last night was inadequate because the bill itself was inadequate, and that steps ought to be taken to improve the bill so as to provide for this supervision. We spend a good deal of the taxpayers' money with regard to insurance companies; or perhaps it is not the taxpayers' money because possibly a levy is made on the insurance companies for the purpose. However, we make a real effort to see that insurance companies in this country are well run.
The minister in his budget told us that he is now going to try to see that pension funds are better run. Here we are starting a new savings scheme on which a great many simple people will depend for their old age. Surely at the very start it would be prudent, wise and foresighted to make adequate provision for the administration and policing of the scheme. It seems to me that is something to which further consideration should be given.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

I have listened with great interest to this discussion. It seems to me that the situation is clear. This is something as to which in its early stage the companies concerned are in touch with the taxation department. Their statements come every year. They pay taxes every year. Surely the officials who are presently engaged in this administration

have the most intimate knowledge of the companies financing in all their details. Certainly if the minister had come along and had announced a great new department being set up, with dozens of people in it, I think we would all have been a little bit critical. I think we would have said "Why are you doing that? You have many competent people. Why do you not build this thing up as it comes?" I do not think anyone would deny that the taxation department takes an interest in the affairs of various companies. I have never heard that questioned. I can see no reason to believe that this situation, as it develops, will not come automatically and inevitably to the attention of the present competent officials and those who will be added as necessity demands.

The hon. member for
Greenwood described his intervention as a question. In a way it was a question and I will attempt to answer it. As he almost always is, I think he was exceedingly reasonable in what he said. I think it would have commended itself to me completely if the Minister of Finance himself had not raised a query in our minds about trustee pension funds in his budget speech. But for the very precise reason that he did that, he raised in everyone's mind the question whether the Department of National Revenue was equipped at the present time or perhaps had the authority at the present time to do this very thing.
As my friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River put it so well last night, it is precisely because of the question that the minister himself, with all his authority and all his knowledge, raised in his own budget speech with respect to trustee pension funds that we have been alerted to this problem. We perhaps would never have thought of raising this question ourselves; as the minister is so fond of telling us, we are such an inefficient opposition, and we do not think of these things ourselves. We perhaps would never have thought of it if the minister had not put the idea in our minds in his budget speech with reference to another form of deferred benefit for which there is an immediate tax abatement. It is precisely for that reason, namely that the minister himself has suggested that there is a deficiency in our existing machinery in respect of a very similar thing, that we feel we should not allow that kind of situation to grow up.
I quite agree with the hon. member for Greenwood. Indeed, I doubt whether there is in this house any other hon. member, since Mr. Thatcher went to another place, who is as concerned about saving the taxpayers' money as I am, with the possible exception of the hon. member for Greenwood, who I

think shares with me a kind of old-fashioned frugal attitude to life. I certainly do not include the Minister of Finance, who has inflated the expenditures of this country out of all recognition since the days when Mr. Harris administered them frugally up to 1957. If Mr. Harris had still been here I would have included him in that select category. But perhaps this semi-biographical material is not very relevant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is very true.

What I am coming back to is this. If this could be done by a very modest improvement in the establishment of the Department of National Revenue; or if the department feels this is not its proper function, as it might, if some arrangement could be made with the superintendent of insurance, who really has much more of this kind of function, to keep an eye on these things, it seems to me that we might avoid a situation which would be regrettable in the future. I make no apology for insisting upon this point.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall paragraph 12 carry?

In connection with this matter of registration may I say this. I recall that some years ago there was some considerable anxiety among officials and ministers as to what responsibility, if any, rested upon the administration simply by the registration of a pension plan. Here we are asking for registration of another form of employees' benefits. If the trustee mismanages that fund we fear registration might involve the government in the same manner as we feared registration might involve the government in some responsibility with the pension plan. What has the minister to say as to the justification for an employee saying, if the fund is mismanaged and the assets are not there when he retires and he complains, "I thought this was a fine fund; it was registered with the government" and who feels that the government is to blame for not having had adequate supervision? I know we discussed this matter with respect to pension plans, the blue book and so on. I am wondering what the minister has to say as to future liability merely by registration without perhaps more supervision.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the hon. member was parliamentary assistant to the minister of finance at the time the statute was amended to strike out the word "approved" as applied to those pension plans and substitute the word "registered". The change emphasized the fact that the government was not to be deemed to be giving approval to the plan or the operations under 90205-6-4961
Income Tax Act
it. This present clause contemplates registration on the conditions described in the subclause. I do not think I can add anything useful to that. The employee who has important rights at stake here will have to take some responsibility on his own shoulders also for seeing that the fund in which he is interested is properly administered, and to that end assuring that there will be a competent trustee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 13 carry?

speechtext:
Subclause agreed to.
On subclause 14.
Will the minister explain the effect of clause 14 (b)?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Putting it briefly, Mr. Chairman, this means that where the registration is revoked the tax advantages die with the revocation and remain in that condition as long as the registration is revoked.
When one of these plans is revoked is there an attempt made immediately to recover the tax over the years on all the funds that have been put into the plan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. The tax advantage that the clause contemplates continues during the period of registration. It begins with the registration; it ends with the revocation of registration. But remember that if the funds are paid out on any other basis than the provisions of the plan, which will contemplate on retirement of the employee, of course the payment out becomes taxable in the hands of the recipient.

Could the minister explain very briefly just what would happen after a plan had been revoked? As far as what had happened between the date of registration and the date of revocation was concerned, would the plan still operate, in so far as the treasury was concerned, as though it had not been revoked? In other words would the revocation merely apply to the future and not in any way to the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The revocation will take effect from its own date. I dealt with this question, Mr. Chairman. I have pointed out that if one of the grounds, or if a ground, upon which the minister proceeded to withdraw or revoke the registration was payment out in breach of the conditions of the plan upon which it had been admitted to registration, then certainly tax would be collected on the payment out in the hands of the recipients.
Subclause 14 agreed to.

Income Tax Act
On subclause 15.

Mr. Chairman, I do not understand the explanatory note, where there is reference to a percentage. The explanatory note says:
-even although it is not expressed as a percentage of profits-
What does the minister have in mind with respect to "percentage of profits"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is a relieving provision. It is designed to make clear that the plan does not have to stipulate in advance for a fixed percentage of the profits of the employer being paid over at the end of the year.
A fixed percentage is really what is involved?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.
Subclause 15 agreed to.
On subclause 16.
What precisely is the purpose of this subclause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Throughout clause 27-as renumbered now, 26-in various places there is the expression "the employee or other beneficiary". This subclause 16 defines the expression "other beneficiary". It says:
-"other beneficiary" shall be construed as meaning any person, other than the employee, to whom any amount is or may become payable by a trustee under the plan-
How can that be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It might be his widow on his death.

I understand that. But there are of course strict provisions, if I remember rightly, against any assignment or any hypothec, or anything of that sort, of any of these funds. So the beneficiary here would only be a beneficiary within the terms of the plan itself; that is to say, at the end of the period of deferment. There could be no beneficiary in the interval, I take it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would have to be a beneficiary defined by the plan, and the terms of the plan must all conform to the terms of the clause before us.

May I put a hypothetical case to the minister. Is it envisaged that these plans would provide that in the case of the death of an employee, whoever his legal heir was would be a beneficiary and would be able to draw upon the fund once the will had been probated or the estate wound up?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot imagine any plan under which the rights of the employee in the fund would terminate on his

death if the payments out to him had not been exhausted as of that date.
The minister does not know of any such plan?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot imagine any plan under which the employee's rights under the fund would terminate on death, if the payments out to him had not then exhausted his interest in the fund.

There are such plans.
Subclause 16 agreed to.

move, Mr. Chairman.

We will now proceed to new clause 28.
On new clause 28-Deductions from income from businesses of associations, etc.
Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister is going to give us some explanation of this clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is clause 29, renumbered 28. This amendment deals with a deduction for drilling and exploration expenses incurred in searching for oil or natural gas. The act at present permits an association, partnership or syndicate formed for the purpose of drilling or exploring for petroleum or natural gas to deduct its drilling and exploration expenses. However, a member of such an association may not deduct his share of these expenses from his income from other sources. This amendment will extend the present concession and permit a taxpayer to apply his share of the expenses from one
Income Tax Act
association or partnership against his income from another association or partnership.
Subclause 2 involves an amendment which deals with bonus payments made to a government for a lease to extract petroleum or natural gas, or for the right to explore for these products. The act at the present time permits-

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I could make a suggestion to the minister. Would it be more convenient, since the subclauses do not seem to be too clearly related, if we could clear up each one separately and then go on to the next? This might save a lot of time. I should like to ask one question in respect to the first provision. Does this involve a relaxation or a tightening up of the law? I must say this is an aspect of the law-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a relieving provision.
That is to say it is another concession or tax benefit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
What is the reason for extending this tax benefit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is fairness and equity, Mr. Chairman, having regard to the purposes which I have indicated.
Well, the minister is suggesting-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are proposing to extend the concession by permitting an individual taxpayer to apply his share of the expenses in one association or partnership against his income from another association or partnership. So in this respect it is a matter of equity, extending to individuals the kind of treatment that has hitherto been accorded to associations, partnerships or syndicates.

Mr. Chairman, what the minister is saying in other words is that the present law is not equitable. Could the minister say when the government discovered that the present law was inequitable, how it discovered that, how this amendment came about, and whether representations have been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should not attempt to pinpoint that for a moment. We receive representations all the time, and these matters are under study at all times.

Is this something in respect of which the government received representations a year ago and did not accept them? Was the inequity maintained all last year?

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is a matter that has been discussed from time to time over some period.

Mr. Chairman, I have been rather interested in this regard because to a simple mind, what is equitable in 1961 should also have been equitable in 1960. The minister is defending this amendment on the basis of fairness and equity, yet he says he has been receiving representations for several years. I think the minister ought to tell us when it dawned upon him that this was inequitable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the observations about what was equity in 1960 will equally apply to 1956 or the early part of 1957. These matters are under study and there are representations received from time to time. They are subjected to very careful study, and we are satisfied now that this amendment should be made, and we so recommend to the committee.

Will this amendment, apart from being equitable, which is, of course, the first concern of the government-that is, justice as between one taxpayer and another -be productive of any advantage to the national interest? Will it result in any greater investment or any greater expansion, shall we say, or is it merely a matter of being equitable as between taxpayers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should expect it to be of particular assistance to individuals who may be interested in drilling and exploration for oil or natural gas. This is a provision which is going to be of assistance to individuals, people of small interests.

Mr. Chairman, when we have dealt with the amendments to section 83 we shall have legislation in two parts, one with respect to drilling for petroleum or natural gas, and then in the same area of the tax statute we have a comparable concession to those engaged in metal mining. What is the situation at the present time in respect to an individual who enters upon exploration activities in so far as metal mining is concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that this form of syndicate or association has prevailed in the gas and oil exploration field but has not been used in relation to metal mining. Certainly we have had no representations from anyone interested in metal mining in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, we were just dealing with the first subclause. The minister had started to explain the second

one, and if no one else has anything to say I should like him to continue his explanation in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the second subclause you will see that this amendment deals with bonus payments made to a government for a lease to extract petroleum or natural gas, or the right to explore for these products. The act at present permits a corporation to deduct such expenditures if the property leased is subsequently abandoned as unproductive. This amendment will extend this right of deduction to a successor corporation which has acquired the property of the corporation which originally made the bonus payment.
What inspired this particular amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Representations and study.
Is this an amendment for the purpose of making the tax more equitable, or is this an incentive to expansion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This again is a relieving provision which should aid in the development of resources.

That is not exactly an answer to my question. I will put each question separately so the minister can explain them separately. Is it felt that this is required because there is some inequity or unfairness in the existing tax structure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is recommended to the house, Mr. Chairman, because it is considered fair and because the government has an interest in encouraging people to concern themselves with exploration. It is thought that this will provide an encouragement to that end.

In what way will it
provide an encouragement? Can the minister explain just what the incentive feature of it is?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think if the hon. member has attempted to follow what I said he will see that it is quite clear. I will go over it again. I have said that the amendment deals with bonus payments made to a government for a lease to extract petroleum or natural gas or for the right to explore for these products. The act at present permits a corporation to deduct such expenditures if the property leased is subsequently abandoned as unproductive. This amendment will extend this right of deduction to a successor corporation which has acquired the property of the corporation which originally made the bonus payment. There are transactions going on

between corporations in this field, those that originally have undertaken the exploration which proved unproductive, and there are naturally tax implications in every one of these transactions. In this case it is thought it will facilitate exploration if the tax benefit that arises in the case where the outlay has proven to be unproductive is available to the successor corporation.

I take it that these bonus payments are payments made to governments other than the federal government, because otherwise there would not seem to be much sense in collecting the bonus payments and then treating them as an expense of doing business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It depends where it is, whether it is in a province or the territories.

Perhaps the minister would explain to me what advantage it would be for the federal government to exact one of these bonus payments if it is going to be given back to the taxpayer, either because he incurred a loss or because he made a gain. In what circumstances could the federal treasury ever get anything out of this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is in a competitive area of competitive business. The hon. member talks about the bonus going back if the venture proves unproductive and treats that as the same situation where an area or property proves productive. He is misleading himself there, Mr. Chairman.
I am not seeking to-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the interests-of equity there are these government charges. I think you will find them imposed by all provinces in the case of exploration carried on within their provincial boundaries. This is the way in which effort is made not only to raise revenues but also to proceed with some regard for equity in relation to the rights that are given by government to persons interested in exploration. This is dealing with the matter at a later stage; this is dealing with the matter after there has been an outlay and after the bonus has been paid to the government for the lease. Later on, if the property leased has been abandoned as unproductive, there is an advantage today taxwise on the part of the lessee, the lessee being a corporation; it is a very considerable advantage to that lessee to be able to convey that position to a successor corporation. It has the opportunity of conveying its interests to another corporation.

Have we not always been very loath to permit corporations to merge, one corporation to buy another corporation
Income Tax Act
largely for a tax reason, such as perhaps a tax loss of considerable substance that one company had on its books? Is not this equivalent to encouraging the buying of one company by another company simply because one company is carrying some losses? Is this not the kind of thing that we do not encourage in a normal way, and indeed discourage as between one corporation and another, one corporation with a substantial profit and another with rather heavy losses? One company is merged with the other simply for tax gain. Is this not doing about the same thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I do not think it is doing the same thing, because this is limited in its application. This applies to the payment made to the government in respect of the lease. I do not think this can be regarded as an inroad on the basic principle of section 83A of the act in that sense.

Mr. Chairman, the minister gave what seemed to me to be a very lucid explanation of this provision as it applied to payments made to some other government. I can see quite clearly that the government, say, of the province of Alberta would get the bonus and the taxpayer would be allowed to treat this bonus, I would think quite properly, as one of the expenses of his operation. But what I cannot get through my head is, if the bonus is paid to the federal government and if the taxpayer is going to be allowed to treat that bonus as an expense of doing business, what conceivable purpose there would be in having the bonus in the first place.

The first subclause of old clause 31 concerns reserves which taxpayers may deduct in computing income. The Income Tax Act, in section 85B (l)(d) provides that if a taxpayer has been required to include an amount in income on account of property sold during the year and the proceeds of the sale are not fully receivable within two years, the taxpayer may deduct as a reserve the amount that can reasonably be regarded as a portion of the profits from the sale. The two year rule is intended to leave out a great number of sales where payment is made over a period shorter than two years. It has been the practice when real estate was sold on a deferred payment basis to bring into income annually that proportion of the profit on the transaction that the payments receive in a year bore to the total sales price.
However, this concession to the taxpayer may not be completely provided for under the present law. Moreover, it has become apparent that some provision should be made to cover the method of operation followed by land development companies. These companies, frequently made up of builders, acquire land, subdivide it, instal services and

sell it to builders. The Department of National Revenue takes the position that a sale is made when a lot is transferred to a builder, but the builder may not be able to make payment for several months. It may extend over the year-end of the land company. This means that the land company has to include in income money it has not actually received, and because the term of the payment does not extend more than two years it does not qualify for a reserve under the present provisions of the act. The amendment provides that a reserve may be deducted with respect to sales of land where the proceeds of the sale are not receivable until after the end of the taxation year.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock on Saturday Your Honour had just drawn my attention to the scope of the bill, and there had been some discussion about a point which I was in the midst of making and which I did not have an opportunity to complete.
The point I was making was this. It is a very simple and a very obvious point, but one about which there seems to be an amazing amount of misunderstanding and confusion, and indeed a very marked change in attitude in the case of one very distinguished person. I refer to the question of who is sovereign in this country.
Lest Your Honour should think I am embarking upon a line of argument that is not germane to the bill, I will deal with that point first. The whole point of the argument I was making following the argument made, without any exception being taken to it, by my hon. friend from Laurier was that since parliament is sovereign in this country, parliament certainly has a right, before granting large sums of money to be expended by a crown corporation, to know who is going to be the head of that corporation and who its directors are going to be. That is the precise objection that we on this side of the house are taking to the government proceeding with this bill without first telling us the answer to that question.
My hon. friend from Laurier on the orders of the day this morning asked the Prime Minister whether the directors and the chairman had yet been appointed as a result of the legislation passed by this house some time ago. I remember very well that the legislation was passed by this house before the famous by-elections, because I made certain predictions about it that I am afraid are not going to be fulfilled quite literally. However, I think they are a fair indication of what is likely to happen in due course with regard to that legislation. I say, as my hon. friend from Laurier has already said, that we as a sovereign parliament are entitled to know who is going to be in charge of this crown corporation, who is going to be spending these millions and millions of dollars, before the taxpayers' money is invested in this fashion. I use the word "invested" because of course these are capital sums with which we are dealing in this bill.
In the days when the present government was not in office and when the right hon. gentleman and some of the other occupants of
Canadian National Railways the treasury benches were over here on this side of the house, this kind of argument in this set of circumstances was very frequently made both inside and outside the house. In order to illustrate the importance of the argument I am making I wish to cite as an authority the Prime Minister himself in the days when he was leader of the opposition.
I recognize that was for a very short period, and therefore I have not many citations. In fact I wish to cite only one. I have in my hand a clipping from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, a newspaper that I find very useful for reference. This is a clipping from that newspaper of March 22, 1957, headed:
Diefenbaker demands reforms-Parliament "puppet of few cabinet ministers".
In an address in Halifax the present Prime Minister appealed for:
Restoration of the prestige of parliament which today "has become the plaything and puppet of a few cabinet ministers".
I suggest that in respect of the Canadian National Railways that is precisely what has happened. Since last September nine months and eleven days have passed during which this government has declined to decide who should be the regularly appointed chairman of the board and who should be the directors of that railway, the greatest railway in North America. It does seem to me that the government, or a few cabinet ministers are treating parliament in exactly the kind of way to which the right hon. gentleman took exception at the time when he was over here on this side of the house. In other words they are seeking to make parliament the puppet of a few cabinet ministers. We are not entitled to know-we are supposed to vote this money blindly-who these people are who are to manage this railway; who is to be the head of the management of the railway; whether Mr. Gordon is finally to get out of the death cell in which he has found himself ever since last September; whether his exit from it is to be to the executioner's block, or whether he is to get a reprieve.

I want to make it very clear, as I think I did the other day and as my hon. triend from Laurier did, that we do not question the right of the government to replace Mr. Gordon. That is their right under the law. And we are not suggesting that parliament should usurp the functions of the government; not at all. What we are suggesting is the government should do what it is supposed to do. It should do it when it is supposed to do it, and then account for its conduct to parliament so parliament can make an intelligent judgment. If the government have found someone better than Mr. Gordon to run this railway, let them appoint him. If they cannot find anyone, let them take Mr. Gordon out of this state of suspense and reappoint him. Either course would be a respectable and a responsible course. The course that is being followed is irresponsible. It is bound to lead to bad morale; it cannot help but do so, and it should not be continued.

Mr. Diefenbaker complained that the prestige of parliament had been dropping because "members were denied information on affairs of the nation".

However, there has been no suggestion on the part of the government that it intends to deviate one whit from the trend that apparently is to be followed, of establishing for ministers of the crown and this government an absolutism.
Those are the words of the present Prime Minister applied to the government of that day in 1955. Those words apply to the Prime Minister today who, when he is asked whether the directors of the Canadian National Railways have been appointed, on a day when the government is coming here theoretically asking us-in fact ordering us-to vote this money, says, "No, you are not entitled to this information". They said it was urgent

to get the bill through so they could appoint the directors and settle Mr. Gordon's fate, yet six weeks afterwards no appointments have been made, no decisions arrived at. Parliament has the right to know these things. As my friend the hon. member for Laurier said the other day, once we in parliament can be got rid of the government can perhaps start leafing through its list of defeated candidates and other supporters of their party to fill up these holes.

I venture to say that no Prime Minister in the history of this country has ever before uttered those words in the House of Commons.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman can make his speech when I have finished mine. He has been of great assistance to me on previous occasions, but on this occasion I can do without that assistance. I suggest to you, sir, that this parliament, has the right to be told, and we have a duty as the opposition to use our resources in this parliament to find out, who are the individuals who will run this railway before we dispose of vast sums of money, millions of dollars, to unknown persons. Indeed, we should not dispose of these vast sums of money to unknown persons.
There is a second point, Mr. Speaker, which seems to me to be very relevant. That is that the government has responsibility for the management of the railway. The government is not charged with management, but parliament has charged the Canadian National Railways under the statute with management. However, the government has the responsibility for the management. The Minister of Finance has denied that the government has any responsibility in another field, but in this field I do not think even the Minister of Finance would deny that he has the ultimate responsibility to this parliament for the deficit. It is not Mr. Gordon who is responsible; the responsibility lies on the Minister of Finance. The government cannot escape that responsibility. If the government is to discharge that responsibility to this parliament as it should be discharged the government must have management of the railway in which it has confidence, and it must back up that management in the way it should be backed up, or it should get rid of it.
I remember very often Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, who had a very different conception of the relationship between the government and parliament and a very different conception of the responsibility of government for agencies under its control, saying in this house that we must either have confidence in the management of the railway or we


must get a new management. That is the only proper way to do it, but this government will not do either. As my hon. friend from Laurier said, it expresses no confidence in the management. It refuses. It continues to sit by and listen to the backbenchers abuse Mr. Gordon and attack the management. It expresses no confidence in the management. It is true the Minister of Transport said that he liked Mr. Gordon and he got on very well with him, but he did not say "We have confidence in Mr. Gordon; we think he is the best man for the job, and we are backing him up".

speechtext: Do you?

That is not my affair; it is the government's affair. The government is responsible. Every time anybody in this house suggests that this government should take responsibility for something they reply, "Do you take responsibility for it?" Why, sir, the Prime Minister was in Winnipeg the other day, and according to news reports he is even blaming the Liberals for the drought. They just cannot take responsibility for anything, not even themselves.
The plain fact is, sir, that whatever one may feel about Mr. Gordon, he has been treated in a shocking way by this government, in what my hon. friend from Laurier has described over and over again as a disgraceful way. If they do not believe in Mr. Gordon, if they think he is no good, they do not need to keep him there; they can let him go and do something else. But if they do think he is the best man they should confirm his appointment and give him the necessary prestige and confidence to carry on this tremendous responsibility. It is a tremendous responsibility to run any railway these days, and to run this greatest of all the railways on the North American continent is one of the biggest jobs on this continent, and one of the most difficult. Surely, if we are going to have any kind of management at all, that management has got to be invested with the confidence and backing of the government.
Of course this is just part of a system. As one well known citizen of this country has said, this is just part of that systematic attack on all crown companies which seems to pervade the ranks of hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not say that the members of the government themselves do it directly, but one knows something from long association with politics and long experience in parliament that the backbenchers do not talk the way they do, they do not make the kind of reports they do, if they are discouraged. I do not say they are encouraged.

I say they betray the real bent of the Prime Minister's mind after four years in office; that the government is sovereign, not parliament.

Canadian National Railways

Perhaps it was in his mind all along; perhaps even four years ago when he said "parliament, the puppet of a few cabinet ministers", he was looking forward to this day. I repeat, sir, there are two things that are shocking about the situation in which we find ourselves in relation to this present bill. The first is that we cannot find out, we are not told, whether the government has any confidence in the present day to day management of the railway, because that is what it is; and that is destructive of morale. The second point is that the government, which undertook as soon as the legislation was through to appoint the remaining directors and the chairman, has not carried out that undertaking to parliament, and is asking us to pass this legislation without that undertaking having been carried out.
Sir, in order to get the opinion of the house on this question I should like now to move an amendment to the second reading of this bill. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith):
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house declines to give second reading to a bill providing large sums for capital expenditures on the railway system while the house is not possessed of the identity of those, namely, the chairman and members of the board of directors, who will be responsible for the making of such expenditures".

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with considerable interest to the speech just made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, and I listened with equal interest to the several statements made on Saturday by some hon. members, notably the hon. member for Laurier. The issue before

us at this moment is a simple one. We are being asked to provide very considerable sums of money under this bill which is to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways system for the period from the 1st day of January, 1961, to the 30th day of June, 1962, and to authorize the guarantee by Her Majesty of certain securities to be issued by the Canadian National Railway Company.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has just contended that before voting these moneys we should learn from the administration what its intentions are with regard to the president, whoever he shall be, of the Canadian National Railways. We are also asking who are to be appointed to fill certain vacancies on the board of directors of this great national railway system. This is not an unusal request under any circumstances, but in the circumstances that now attend the situation with regard to the direction of this railroad I think our justification for asking for this information is great.
We are reminded that the term of office of the president of Canadian National Railways, Mr. Donald Gordon, expired some nine months ago, and that he has been carrying on, I think one may say, on sufferance during this period without any indication whether or not his term of office is to be extended of whether in fact he is to be reappointed for a fixed term under the statute. The Canadian National Railways is a large operation, the largest railway system in the world, yet for some reason this government refuses to indicate whether it proposes to continue the present president in the direction of this railroad. That is an impossible situation.
There are limits on the prerogatives, even by custom, to which a government can legitimately cling. No government can be forced to announce the appointment of a particular individual unless it has been given ample opportunity to make up its mind. But that cannot be contended in this case, because the definite term of the president expired nine months ago. Is it fair to this railway system, is it fair to this parliament, is it fair to this country that this uncertainty should prevail?
The hon. member for Bovavista-Twillingate says you have asked for certain moneys, and before those moneys are granted we are entitled to know who is going to direct the operations connected with the moneys to be appropriated under this bill. This is a reasonable request. I well remember, during the course of another debate this session, attacks were made on the president of the Canadian National Railways largely by members who sit

behind the treasury benches. The Minister of Transport was Anally prevailed upon to come to the defence of an official who serves under him.
It took some pressure to convince the Minister of Transport that it was not fair for a minister to refrain from commenting on attacks that had been made on an official who reports to parliament through him. Finally, after a long and protracted debate, the Minister of Transport manfully acknowledged that as far as he was concerned he had nothing but high commendation for the president of Canadian National Railways. But he qualified his tribute by saying "as far as I am concerned". The hon. gentleman did to an extent meet the tradition that it is always incumbent upon a minister to defend a public official with whom he has official connections, but the minister would not go further than to say "as far as I am concerned".
What we are entitled to know now is what is the regard that this government has for the president of Canadian National Railways? It can express its view as to his competence by giving us some definite indication of what it intends to do by way of reappointment or by way of replacement, but surely we are entitled to have this information. Why has the government not made up its mind, if that is the situation? If it has made up its mind, why should it not tell this house? If it has not made up its mind, then it surely owes to parliament some explanation for this long delay in determining if Mr. Donald Gordon is the kind of man it wishes to see continued as the president of Canadian National Railways.
There is a further principle involved. It is connected with other situations that have nothing to do, of course, with the operation of the railroad. It is that more and more in this country there is a growing feeling, justified or not, that the government is not satisfied with the heads of certain crown corporations, with certain leading public servants.

Order. I question whether the course which the hon. member is following is relevant to this fairly narrow question. The question is the voting of funds for Canadian National Railways and the amendment has placed before the house a very precise reason for not voting those funds, namely, that the house has not been given the names of the chairman and members who will have responsibility for making expenditures. I would think that to discuss the views of the country at large on the government's attitude toward1 other public servants is not relevant to this issue.
Canadian National Railways

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.

I cannot quarrel with the position that you take, except that this was not my main argument. I was surely entitled, in commenting upon the substance of what I have to say, to relate my remarks to the general disquiet which I believe exists with regard to the government's treatment of certain public officials of our country. It was only in that context that I had made my observations.
We have been told in another place by one distinguished senator who happens to be the president of the Progressive Conservative party, that the government has intentions with regard to the division of functions at the top of the management of Canadian National Railways. The suggestion has been made that the office of president will be filled by one individual and that he will not continue as chairman of the board. This is a very important announcement to have come from someone who may be close to the administration but has no official functions whatever in so far as the government of Canada is concerned. We are entitled to know whether or not that announcement of policy from that quarter represents what the government really has in mind.
Does the government intend to divide the functions, as was announced by Senator Thorvaldson or was Senator Thorvaldson talking through his hat? Was he talking with justification or had he been informed of this by the government? Surely it is not treating parliament fairly to suggest that that kind of announcement can be made in another place but that we may not expect any comment on it from a member of the government in this chamber. Surely we are entitled to know, not only if the present president is going to be continued in office, but whether his functions are going to be divided as Senator Thorvaldson indicated.
The Minister of Transport is now in his seat. He has not had the advantage of listening to the earlier part of the discussion. I would tell him, therefore, that we have been arguing here, notably today through the rather moderate but vigorous statement of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate who has presented an amendment, that before we accede to the request for certain moneys as contained in this bill we should be advised what the government's intentions are with regard to continuing in the office of president the present incumbent. We have pointed out that nine months have elapsed since the term of Mr. Gordon came to an end, and that it is wholly irresponsible for the government, after nine months, not to be in a position to indicate what its intentions are as to the replacement of Mr. 7872	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways Gordon or his continuing in office or dividing the functions at the top level of the management of the railroad system.
How long does the government intend to allow this situation of uncertainty to persist? Is there any obligation on the government to make up its mind with regard to this matter? I will admit that the Minister of Transport has not been minister of transport very long.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I wish some other ministers were equally effective. I am not going to name the Minister of Veterans Affairs when I say that, but I simply say I wish the Minister of Transport had some other colleagues who deserved the designation the Minister of Veterans Affairs says applies in this particular case.
The Minister of Transport has not been in office for the full period of these nine months. However, he has been in office now long enough to know what the situation is. He, himself, has said he has confidence in the present president of Canadian National Railways. He made that statement, as I pointed out a few minutes ago, only after considerable prodding. He will remember that for two days strong criticism had been levelled in this house against Mr. Gordon, notably by hon. gentlemen who sit behind the minister. It was only after we had pointed out repeatedly that there was an obligation on the part of the minister either to agree with those criticisms or to defend the president of the railway, that the minister's statement was made. If he agreed with the criticisms, then it was clear what the responsibility of the government with regard to Mr. Gordon must be. The minister is satisfied. He has given the present president full endorsation. No one could have paid a more generous tribute to the competence of Mr. Gordon than did the Minister of Transport.
What we are entitled to know today is whether or not that tribute in appreciation of Mr. Gordon's competence is shared by his colleagues in the government, and whether or not they intend to continue that gentleman in office. This is the gist of the amendment that is before the house at the present time. The amendment deals also with the members of the board of directors who have yet to be appointed. I ask the Minister of Transport, and I ask the Minister of Finance-I would simply say in passing that if the Minister of Finance feels he is being unduly detained in this house, and on that account cannot accept the invitation which has been extended to him in the other place-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: There has been no invitation, so do not litter the record again with untruths.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.

speechtext: I did not catch that last observation, Mr. Speaker, and I like to hear what you say.

speechtext:
I am not going to pursue the point, Mr. Speaker, except to say, with great respect, that I find it difficult to accede to that suggestion. But under the circumstances there may be some other way of dealing with it. I would think it was most extraordinary that in the course of the debate one was precluded from saying to an hon. member that he could absent himself for particular purposes. I find it difficult to accede to the suggestion that such is not the case. However, I have such great respect for Your Honour and for the sensitivity of all the circumstances implied in what I have said that, for the time being, I am prepared to

pass on to my plea to the Minister of Transport. In doing so, however, I cannot help but note how sensitive the Minister of Finance is. I say this to the Minister of Transport. Surely he cannot now take the position that he can go on denying to us knowledge of the government's intention, particularly when we are now approaching the end of the present session or the present portion of this session of parliament. Is the government going to take the position that it will make an announcement with regard to the president of the railroad and the nomination of the new directors after parliament will have risen and before parliament returns? Is the government going to take advantage of that interval to announce if Mr. Gordon is going to be retained and who the new directors are? If that is the decision the government proposes to take I will say now that it will be a demonstration of this government's disregard for parliament. Or let the minister tell us frankly, "We are not in a position to announce it. We have certain considerations in mind that have not yet been realized. We cannot tell the house who the new president is going to be or whether Mr. Gordon is going to be continued or who the new directors are to be." Let the minister take the house into his confidence. But to deny us this information at this time is incomprehensible.
Let the people of this country recognize and recall the fact that we are not asking for something to be settled that has only suddenly arisen but rather something that has been in existence now for almost nine months. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate took the position that before money was granted parliament had the right to know who was going to be the head of the Canadian National Railways. This morning we were told by the Prime Minister that the government had not yet decided who was going to be the president. When is that matter going to be decided? Are we then going to be denied this information only to be confronted when we leave here with a revelation of information that is now being denied to the house? Some hon. members who are new to this chamber find it irritating to find those of us in the Liberal opposition persistently making arguments of this kind. If they will look over the record of Hansard they will see the kind of arguments that were made by the present Minister of Finance and the present Prime Minister, without having anything like the justification that attends us in this particular instance. Because we are asking for what I think it is our duty to ask, we are being criticized and hon. members opposite find our interventions irritating and annoying. They may be annoying and they may be irritating but these are the instruments
Canadian National Railways which an opposition is entitled to use in order to elicit from a reluctant executive information which the public and parliament are entitled to have.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. In the first place I might say I object strenuously, as I indicated earlier, to this matter of seating, but I understand it is under review by the committee of the house. The point I wanted to raise and direct to the attention of the hon. member for Essex East is that the information I was conveying to him is readily available to all hon. members-in fact, to the rest of the world- because it is in the Canadian National annual report, which indicates that Mr. Donald Gordon is the president. This should answer the question contained in this very important motion raised at this time.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Who is the chairman of the board?

speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member, who has crossed the chamber to sit in a seat he prefers, will recognize that he has not raised a question of privilege. However I do not make any comment on that. I can understand what the hon. member is trying to do in not being in his seat; he is trying to get as far away as he can from the ministerial benches. I can well understand why.
The situation is quite clear. In the face of what has been alleged today I hope the Minister of Transport, who comes to this debate fresh, perhaps with information which is not now in the possession of the Minister of Finance, will be able to give us the information to which we are entitled. He was not in the house when the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate read his amendment and therefore I should like to read it again:
This house declines to give second reading to a bill providing large sums for capital expenditures on the railway system while the house is not possessed of the identity of those, namely, the

chairman and members of the board of directors, who will be responsible for the making of such expenditures.
Our request, our justified demand is embodied in the terms of this amendment and by no contrivance possible can the ministry justify refusing to give the house this information. The government is entitled to these moneys in support of the railway, but there must be an answer to our questions. To ask us to vote moneys when the government does not know who is going to head the railway, or when it refuses to give this information, is wholly irresponsible and is in keeping with the disregard for parliament which this government continues to demonstrate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: I make that statement, Mr. Speaker, so there will be no misunderstanding of the situation. There will be opportunity for fair discussion, serious discussion, but there is not time for wilful obstruction and filibuster.

speechtext: Give us the information for which we are asking.

speechtext: The information hon. members need to have will be forthcoming in answers to inquiries they may wish to make on the clauses of the bill. That information will be forthcoming. But I just wish to sound this word of warning to hon. members opposite.

speechtext:
Oh, oh.
Canadian National Railways

If they wish to continue to be irresponsible about this and ignore the position of the Canadian National Railways and the need on the part of the Canadian National Railways for having the financial provisions this bill contains for the railway, they can go ahead and do injustice to the Canadian National Railways and deprive that crown corporation of the provisions it needs from this bill.
The situation is just that, Mr. Speaker. So they can make their choice now between going gaily ahead with their filibuster and denying to the Canadian National Railways provisions which that company now requires, or on the other hand they can deal responsibly with the bill. We can have a serious and sensible discussion without obvious delay, endless repetition, deliberate filibuster and obstruction.

opposite seem to think that just by sheer repetition they are going to compel the government to embark upon-

speechtext: To make up its mind.

-a course that is not within the power of the government to follow at this moment without further steps being taken. speechtext:
The Minister of Finance then made the threat that further discussion in respect to this bill would in some way jeopardize the position of the Canadian National Railways, because it would not have the funds available for this capital work. Let me point out to him that if that is so he owes an apology to the House of Commons for coming to parliament with this legislation so late. If what he has said is true, and is the whole truth, as he put it, then the government has failed in its responsibility in bringing this legislation forward so late that it cannot be considered properly by the house.
To show just how far the minister has gone let me say this. When my desk mate, the hon. member for Essex East was speaking in support of the amendment to the motion, the minister referred to his argument as an inane argument. I should like to follow up the hon. minister's remarks in that regard.
Let me analyse just exactly what he is asking this government to do. He is asking this house to approve a bill providing some $178,900,000 for the Canadian National Railways for purposes more particularly set out in the bill. I remind the Minister of Finance that that represents $10 out of the pocket of each citizen of Canada; those who work, those who are too young to work, and those who are unable to work because of illness. That is the magnitude of this bill. The amount of money asked for is the equivalent of $30 from the pocket of each member of the labour force. That is the amount he is asking the taxpayers to provide this year as well as that enormous amount of money required to offset the budget deficit.
Surely this is a matter of major importance to the citizens of this country. Surely if the Minister of Finance is asking the taxpayers to make this substantial contribution out of their earnings in one year he has an

obligation to tell the taxpayers why he wants that money, because this bill certainly has the effect of arbitrarily taking that money from them.
If the Minister of Finance is going to tell the whole truth, as he refers to it, is he going to tell the taxpayers that he will not inform them who is going to be in charge of spending this vast amount of money? Is he not going to tell them who is to be responsible? Is he going to tell them if they search through the statute books they will find there a board of directors and a chairman of the board, but that he will not tell them who they are? Is he going to tell them that this government will not indicate what its policy is in this regard? Is he going to tell them that if they look at the statute and read it carefully they will find that the government has the right to make these appointments but that the government is going to take this money from the taxpayers without telling them who the management is to be, and only after the government has received the money will it then tell who is to manage the railway?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Parliament be damned.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Surely that is not a responsible way to treat the taxpayers of Canada. Surely that is not a responsible way to treat the members of the House of Commons who, in the final analysis, are nothing more or less than those individuals elected by the voters of Canada to represent the taxpayers. Surely it is not inane to ask the Minister of Finance to reveal the policy of the government in this regard and to reveal the government's action before parliament joins in taking this very large sum of money from the taxpayers for this purpose.

He wonders why we should dare to try to maintain the responsibility of parliament. He wonders why we should attempt to make the government answerable to parliament. The Minister of Transport has made it clear that the government proposes to appoint promptly the members to the board of the directors of the Canadian National Railways and also that the chairman of the board had the support of the government. This was exactly the pattern followed by the Minister of Finance in that other connection. Then the Prime Minister entered the picture. I am wondering if in a few weeks the Minister of Transport will not be forced to take the same type of action vis-a-vis the four directors whose term of office is expiring shortly, and the chairman of the board of directors, as the Minister of Finance was forced to take a few weeks ago vis-a-vis the head of the Bank of Canada. It seems to me that is the kind of situation we are confronted with today. I believe we would be remiss in our duty if we did not press the government of the day to give an explanation regarding the appointment of the men who will be responsible for the direction and administration of this great railway system. Surely that elementary information should be given before this money is provided. I suggest it is an impertinence on the part of the government to go to the taxpayers of Canada and take from them this vast sum of money without giving that information. It is an impertinence to parliament for the Minister of Finance to submit this bill without being ready and willing to give such information.
For my part I completely repudiate the criticism of the Minister of Finance that we are conducting an obvious filibuster. I regard the proceedings in respect to this legislation and the way in which this government is putting it through as an obvious demonstration of arrogance on the part of the government toward parliament. I regard it as the duty of members of parliament to endeavour to obtain this information before this large sum of money is provided from the taxpayers' pockets.

Canadian National Railways in time to hear the proposed amendment. I like to think that I usually speak in moderate terms but I find it difficult to do so this afternoon because, quite frankly, I find it impossible to understand how a serious man could propose such an amendment.

speechtext: Do not let us be led astray by the fact that there are large amounts of money involved. The question is whether this proposal has come before us with the proper authorization. This proposal comes to us from the railway. It does not creep up out of the ground. It has not come in any accidental way. It has been approved by the board of the railway, and the president of the railway came and presented it; then it was discussed by a responsible committee of this house. It was then reduced to legislation and it comes to us with the imprimatur of that committee. In that sense, as I said, it is routine. I have sat on the other side of the house and I have taken part in discussion of this legislation and I have made comments on it but I do not think it ever occurred to me previously that we were acting in an almost irresponsible way and asking the House of Commons to dig up huge amounts of money. What I thought we were doing was coming to the House of Commons, following the careful and responsible sittings of the railway committee, such as took place this year. What is suggested? It is suggested that by reason of an accident, an accidental situation, namely that there are four directors still to be appointed and that the president's appointment, which has expired, has not been repeated yet, in some way that means that we should not vote the amount. It is difficult to understand, as I say, why reasonable men would suggest that. Do they think if we do not know the names today that we will wake up tomorrow morning and find that a lot of third-rate people have been appointed to this board?

speechtext: Of course you are entitled to ask. You have asked it a dozen times. I have never objected to your trying to do that. Incidentally, I have spoken in favour of the president of the railway. I think he is a great executive. That is another matter. It has nothing whatever to do with this. I maintain that these two things are just as far apart as the east is from the west. We have here a bill which came to us following the deliberations of a serious committee. It is a thing which, as I say, is routine, and in the sense in which I use the terms the hon. member admits it. It comes up every year. Are hon. members to say that because there are still four directors to be appointed and the president's appointment has not yet been continued the money is not to be spent but is to be held back? As I say, it is difficult for me to understand how serious men would ever make such a proposal, it is such a trivial argument. One might go on and argue that the eight men who are on that board now no doubt, were a party to these amounts being produced before the committee and that the committee sent on the measure now before us. Incidentally, those eight men would still be an effective majority on the board. However, that is a trivial argument and I do not make much of that. I return to my original point. This is a measure in the ordinary course of business, sanctioned by our practice year after year. In my view it is trivial to suggest that this measure should not be passed because we have not got the full list of members of the board of directors. Do we think that a lot of wild men are going to be appointed? Do we think that some men utterly incompetent to run the railway are going to be appointed? No, of course we do not.
